article_text:
ドクメンタ16がキュレーションチームを拡充。一方でガザ問題等をめぐり参加辞退の作家も

5年に一度 ドイツ で開催される国際的美術展 ドクメンタ は、2027年に第16回目を迎える。このドクメンタ16で芸術監督を務めるナオミ・ベックウィズが、4人の新たなキュレーションメンバーを指名した。昨年発表された、ドクメンタ史上初の女性だけのキュレーターチームを拡充するものになる。

10月29日、 ドクメンタ 16の芸術監督ナオミ・ベックウィズがキュレーションチームの拡充を発表した。レイヴン・チャコンが特別キュレーターを務め、オセイ・ボンス、ティメア・ユングハウス、ノーム・セガールがキュレーション顧問に就任する。

チャコンは北米 先住民 ディネ族のアーティストで、作曲家、ミュージシャンとしても活動し、2022年に先住民アーティストとして初めて ピューリッツァー賞 （音楽部門）を受賞。2017年には、アートコレクティブ「ポストコモディティ」のメンバーとしてドクメンタ14に参加した。

ボンスはガーナ系イギリス人の美術史家で、現在は ロンドン の テート・モダン で アフリカ およびアフリカンディアスポラに関する国際的アート分野のシニアキュレーター職にある。

美術史家でキュレーターのユングハウスは、「ヨーロッパの（エスニックマイノリティである）シンティとロマの現代美術・批評的思考に関する分野の第一人者」と発表資料で紹介されている。2017年から25年まで ベルリン にある欧州ロマ芸術文化研究所の初代事務局長を務め、2007年には ヴェネチア・ビエンナーレ 初のロマ・パビリオンのキュレーションを担当した。

セガールは、テクノロジーを用いた現代アートを専門とするキュレーター兼研究者だ。現在は ニューヨーク の グッゲンハイム美術館 で、アソシエイトキュレーターおよびLGグッゲンハイム賞の選考委員を務めている。

今回の発表にあたり、グッゲンハイム美術館の副館長で、チーフキュレーターでもあるベックウィズはこう述べている。

「彼らのような卓越したクリエイターや研究者と共に仕事ができることを、非常に嬉しく思っています。4人の信念の揺るぎなさは、共同作業への取り組みにおいても同じです」

ベックウィズは昨年8月、女性だけで構成されるキュレーションチームを発表した。これは70年にわたるドクメンタの歴史初の決定で、メンバーに名を連ねるのはカーラ・アセベド=イェーツ、ロミ・クロフォード、マイラ・A・ロドリゲス・カストロ、シャオユー・ウェン（翁小雨）の4人だ。

次回のドクメンタ16は、2027年6月12日から9月19日まで ドイツ ・カッセル市内の各会場で開催を予定。そのプレスリリースには、「本展および関連プログラムは、激動の世界を歩み、地球規模の不確実性の中で共に生きるための戦略や新たな可能性を切り拓こうとするアーティストたちに敬意を表するものです。即興、実験、そして集団的な学びが新たな道を開くでしょう」と記されている。

その一方、9月にベックウィズは独ディー・ツァイト紙に対し、ドクメンタ16への参加を打診されたうち複数のアーティストが辞退したことを明らかにした。その理由について彼女は、「ドイツでは、自分たちが見せたいものを自由に表現できないのではないかという印象を抱いているケースもあれば、 ガザ地区 の紛争に対するドイツの姿勢に批判的な作家もいます」と説明している。

前回、2022年のドクメンタ15では、展示や参加アーティストの一部に反ユダヤ主義的な傾向があると一部の政治家が主張して物議を醸した。これを受けてドクメンタ側は、反ユダヤ主義について明記した新しい行動規範を採択。その中で、 イスラエル に対する批判は「人種差別的な試み」とされている。（翻訳：石井佳子）

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Two-time Oscar winner Renée Zellweger will play a faded TV actress who gets a shot at redemption in the real world in Sacha Gervasi-directed high concept comedy drama, Darlington , which will be kicking off foreign sales at AFM . A spring production next year in the UK is in the works.

The Rocket Science, Monumental Pictures, and Portobello Electric production also stars BAFTA Award nominee Dominic Sessa ( The Holdovers, Tony ) and longtime Gervasi collaborator Peter Dinklage (who is making village women’s dreams true on the big screen in Black Bear’s critically acclaimed sex comedy, Wicker ).

Related Stories

Four 'Star Trek' Vets Reunite For Sci-Fi 'Life 2.0', OneTwoThree Media Launches AFM Sales; Brit Comedy With Stephen Fry, Jane Horrocks Also On Slate

Tracee Ellis Ross, Lake Bell & Ken Leung Thriller 'Blow The Horn' Heads To AFM For Sales

Gervasi penned the screenplay which follows the Judy and Cold Mountain Oscar winner as Kate Spencer, an actress long forgotten by the industry, but is invited to reprise her most famous role — not in a revival of the show, but in the actual world where a reclusive tech billionaire (Sessa) has meticulously restored an English country estate to its former glory. Having retreated from the world, he now lives his life there in the fantasy that it is actually 1923. As Kate settles into this strange, controlled existence, she discovers that illusion and reality are far more entwined than she ever imagined.

Watch on Deadline

Darlington is produced by Alison Owen ( Ghosts, Back To Black, Me Before You, Saving Mr Banks ) and Debra Hayward ( Ghosts, Bridget Jones Baby, Les Miserables ) of Monumental Pictures, and Jim Garavente ( Game Night ) is producing for Portobello Electric. The film is executive produced by Alexander Payne ( The Holdovers, Sideways ).

Zellweger recently starred in and executive produced the final chapter in the Bridget Jones’ franchise Mad About the Boy and is currently in production on the feature film A Woman in the Sun.

Following his critically acclaimed turn in Tony, Sessa is currently filming Miami Vice ’85.

Gervasi is an award-winning British writer and director whose career spans independent filmmaking, major studio features and prestige television. He co-wrote Steven Spielberg’s $219M-plus grossing The Terminal , starring Tom Hanks and Catherine Zeta-Jones. Gervasi made his directorial debut with the critically acclaimed hit, Anvil! The Story of Anvil (2008). Premiering at Sundance, it won the Independent Spirit Award for Best Documentary. He subsequently directed the Academy Award-nominated Hitchcock , starring Anthony Hopkins, Helen Mirren and Scarlett Johansson, with Mirren earning BAFTA, Golden Globe and SAG Award nominations for her performance. Gervasi also wrote and directed the critically lauded My Dinner with Hervé , starring Dinklage, Jamie Dornan and Andy Garcia for HBO, earning a Primetime Emmy nomination for Outstanding Television Movie, alongside nominations from the Critics’ Choice Awards, Producers Guild of America, and Writers Guild of America.

Zellweger is represented by CAA. Sessa is represented by CAA and Untitled Entertainment. Gervasi is represented by CAA and Kaplan / Perrone Entertainment. Dinklage is repped by CAA and Jackoway Austen Tyerman etc.

article_text:
Films and events

Love

The Slightest Touch

The power of friendship and connection is explored in Rachel Fleit’s soulful and life-affirming documentary, featuring Emma Fogarty and Colin Farrell.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director Rachel Fleit

USA-Ireland 2026. 103min

Courtesy of HBO Max

Language English

Access information

Monday 12 October 20:45

Descriptive subtitles

Thursday 15 October 16:00

Descriptive subtitles

Find out about booking access tickets

Introduction

Emma lives with Epidermolysis Bullosa (EB), the slightest touch causing her skin to blister and tear. To celebrate her 40th, she runs a marathon with longtime pal, Colin, raising awareness of this shamefully understudied condition. Defying the odds with grit and humour, this dynamic duo’s race to the finish is an inspirational ode to friendship and being open to the world and all that it offers.

Kristy Matheson

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

Being Heumann

British actor Ruth Madeley is outstanding as Judith Heumann, the activist who helped fight for anti-discrimination laws for individuals with disabilities, in CODA director Siân Heder’s enthralling film.

Adam Pearson: Zero Intention of Living Quietly

Actor, broadcaster, and leading disability advocate Adam Pearson joins us to discuss his career and his influential advocacy work for more inclusive storytelling and authentic representation.

Petrolheads

Life can feel like a Western in this warm buddy movie, in which neurodiverse Martin and Casper search for their perfect car: the 1994 Honda Civic.

"paragraph", "text": "在备受瞩目的《X战警》电影系列中，斯图尔特饰演泽维尔教授，与饰演反派万磁王的好友伊恩·麦克莱恩演对手戏。他将在今年12月上映的《复仇者联盟：末日之战》中与麦克莱恩再度携手，重演该角色。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在2008年的一篇人物专访中，斯图尔特谈到了自己重回古典戏剧根基主演《麦克白》的经历，《纽约时报》在其巧妙融梗的标题中精辟地概括了这位演员职业生涯中走过的两条截然不同的道路：“去莎士比亚召唤的浩瀚深处。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "除了曾获得4项艾美奖提名外，斯图尔特还凭借戏剧表演荣获3项劳伦斯·奥利弗奖，并获得过托尼奖提名。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "怎么强调斯图尔特的生活在1987年开始出演《星际迷航：下一代》时发生多么剧烈的变化都不为过。在此之前的二十年里，他一直是皇家莎士比亚剧团的中流砥柱。尽管他曾抽空参与一些电影和电视工作，但大部分时间都忙于演出两打以上的皇家莎士比亚剧团舞台剧，其中包括1974年在《万尼亚舅舅》中饰演阿斯特罗夫、1977年在《仲夏夜之梦》中饰演奥伯龙、1978年在《威尼斯商人》中饰演夏洛克，以及1981年在《泰特斯·安特罗尼克斯》中饰演同名主角。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "斯图尔特在1987至1994年播出的《星际迷航：下一代》全剧中一直饰演皮卡德，随后又出演了电影《星际迷航：世代》（与威廉·夏特纳同台）、《星际迷航：第一次接触》、《星际迷航：起义》和《星际迷航：复仇女神》。他还在《X战警》（2000）、《X战警2》、《X战警：背水一战》、《X战警前传：金刚狼》、《金刚狼》和《X战警：逆转未来》中饰演泽维尔教授。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在评价斯图尔特对《星际迷航：下一代》的贡献时，《纽约时报》写道：“凭借其严厉而不失公正的威严感和严肃的宗旨感，斯图尔特先生让让-吕克·皮卡德舰长成为了跨越7个季度的《星际迷航：下一代》的道德核心，帮助该剧免于滑向低俗或自我戏仿。好莱坞接纳了他，他也接纳了好莱坞。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "总体而言，斯图尔特对自己的流行文化标签始终保持着良好的幽默感，从未公开流露出夏特纳和伦纳德·尼莫伊有时曾表现出的那种焦虑。他曾为《辛普森一家》、《恶搞之家》和《美国老爹》配音，并表现出勇于涉足喜剧领域的意愿：在史蒂夫·马丁1991年的佳作《洛杉矶故事》中饰演了一位滑稽势利的侍应生，在梅尔·布鲁克斯1993年的《罗宾汉疯狂滑稽秀》中饰演理查德国王，并于1994年主持了《周六夜现场》。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他最近在动画片《羊探》中为里奇菲尔德爵士配音。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在截然不同的领域里，他是1995年同性恋题材喜剧片《杰弗里》中的最大亮点；《纽约时报》评价斯图尔特称，“他拥有一些最精彩的台词，并以一种尊贵而有气势的风格将它们演绎出来，而当他碰巧戴着一顶紫红色贝雷帽时——那是一个名为‘粉红豹’的反同性恋暴力团体的制服——这种效果更是得到了进一步的提升。”后来，这位演员还担任了塞思·麦克法兰尖刻喜剧《Ted》及其续集的旁白。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "斯图尔特出演了2015年由斯蒂芬·贝尔伯的戏剧改编的电影《对局》，在片中饰演了一位虚荣、浮夸的舞蹈教练；而在截然不同的惊悚片领域，他还出演了杰瑞米·索尔尼尔的恐怖惊悚片《绿色房间》，在片中饰演了一群新纳粹分子团伙的头目。他还主演了Starz电视台的剧集《布朗特谈话》，饰演了一位搬到洛杉矶主持脱口秀的有药瘾的英国新闻主播。", "translated": true}, {"type": article_text:
Patrick Stewart , the English actor with impressive stage and film credits who will be remembered most for his roles as Captain Jean-Luc Picard on “ Star Trek: The Next Generation ” and as Professor Charles Xavier in the “ X-Men ” films, died Wednesday at his Los Angeles home. He was 86.

According to a statement on his Instagram account, Stewart died after a brief battle with Alzheimer’s and Lewy Body Dementia.

“His sonorous voice and singular talent will forever be synonymous with indelible performances in every genre. He explored the human condition in all its poetic complexity and brought hope not only to the far reaches of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, but into science fiction’s most iconic final frontier aboard the Starship Enterprise,” the statement read. “His professional accomplishments were humbly matched by his philanthropy and activism on behalf of human rights, survivors of domestic violence, global refugees, veterans’ mental health services, and animal welfare, particularly his cherished foster pitties. He was a Knight, Chancellor, motor sport enthusiast, and lifelong Huddersfield Football fan. He will be remembered for the dignity, compassion and humanity he brought to every role — in his art and life.”

Stewart and his “Star Trek: TNG” co-stars took their characters to the big screen for several films before the “Star Trek” film franchise was rebooted by J.J. Abrams with characters from the original series. He returned to the franchise for “Star Trek: Picard,” which ran from 2020 to 2023.

In the high-profile “X-Men” film franchise, Stewart played Professor Xavier opposite his good friend Ian McKellen as the villainous Magneto. He reprises the role in this December’s “Avengers: Doomsday” alongside McKellen.

In a 2008 profile describing Stewart’s return to his roots in classical theater by starring in a production of “Macbeth,” the New York Times in its mash-up headline pithily referenced the two very different paths the actor had followed in his career: “To Boldly Go Where Shakespeare Calls.”

In addition to being nominated for four Emmy awards, Stewart won three Olivier awards for his theater work and was nominated for a Tony Award.

It is hard to emphasize enough how dramatically Stewart’s life changed when he began his run on “Star Trek: The Next Generation” in 1987. For the two decades prior he had been a mainstay of the Royal Shakespeare Company. He had made time for some film and television work, but was kept busy appearing in more than two dozen RSC stage productions, including as Astrov in “Uncle Vanya” in 1974, Oberon in “A Midsummer Night’s Dream” in 1977, Shylock in “The Merchant of Venice” in 1978, and in the title role in “Titus Andronicus” in 1981.

Stewart played Picard throughout the 1987-1994 run of “Star Trek: TNG,” and then in the features “Star Trek: Generations” (in which he appeared with William Shatner), “Star Trek: First Contact,” “Star Trek: Insurrection” and “Star Trek: Nemesis.” He played Professor Xavier in “X-Men” (2000), “X-Men 2,” “X-Men: The Last Stand,” “X-Men Origins: Wolverine,” “The Wolverine” and “X-Men: Days of Future Past.”

Assessing Stewart’s contributions to “Star Trek: TNG,” the New York Times said, “With his aura of stern yet fair authority and seriousness of purpose, Mr. Stewart made Capt. Jean-Luc Picard the moral center of ‘Star Trek: The Next Generation’ across seven seasons, helping to keep it from sliding into camp or self-parody. Hollywood took to him, and he took to Hollywood.”

In general, Stewart seemed to keep a good sense of humor about his ties to popular culture, never publicly displaying the angst that Shatner and Leonard Nimoy each revealed at times. He did voicework on “The Simpsons,” “Family Guy” and “American Dad” and showed a willingness to make forays into comedy, playing a comically snooty waiter in Steve Martin’s 1991 gem “L.A. Story” and King Richard in Mel Brooks’ 1993 “Robin Hood: Men in Tights,” and hosting “Saturday Night Live” in 1994.

He recently voiced Sir Ritchfield in the animated “Sheep Detectives.”

In a very different vein, he was the best thing in 1995 gay comedy “Jeffrey”; the New York Times said Stewart “has some of the best lines and delivers them with a dignified brio that is only enhanced when he happens to be wearing a fuchsia beret, the uniform of an anti-gay-bashing group called the Pink Panthers.” Later the actor would serve as the narrator for Seth McFarlane’s scabrous comedy “Ted” and its sequel.

Stewart appeared in the 2015 film “Match,” based on the play by Stephen Belber, in which the actor played a vain, flamboyant dance instructor and — in a very different vein — in the Jeremy Saulnier horror-thriller “Green Room,” in which he played the leader of a band of neo-Nazis. He also starred in the Starz series “Blunt Talk,” about a substance-abusing English newscaster who moves to L.A. to host a talkshow.

Stewart continued his stage work even during the run of “Star Trek: TNG,” playing George in “Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?” at the Young Vic in 1987 (he would return to the role at Minneapolis’ Guthrie Theatre in 2001) and repeatedly appearing in seasonal stagings in Los Angeles and on Broadway of a one-man version of “A Christmas Carol” that he adapted himself from the original Dickens.

After “TNG” ended, Stewart ramped up his theater work. He appeared on Broadway as Prospero in “The Tempest” in 1996, essayed the title role in a “photo-negative” staging of “Othello” at the Shakespeare Theatre in Washington, D.C., in 1997 and returned to Broadway to star in “The Ride Down Mt. Morgan” in 2000. In Britain, his work on the boards, starring in “Antony and Cleopatra,” in “The Tempest” and soon triumphing in “Macbeth,” won back the critics who had written him off when he had ventured into American television’s version of outer space years earlier. Also in 2008, Stewart played Claudius in a production of “Hamlet” that starred David Tennant, winning Stewart the Olivier award for best supporting actor.

Stewart had had a productive association with McKellen. In addition to starring as adversaries in the “X-Men” films, during the filming of which they developed a close friendship, the pair appeared on the West End in “Waiting for Godot” in 2009 and in repertory on Broadway in 2014 in that Beckett play and another existential classic, Harold Pinter’s “No Man’s Land.”

The actor made his first cinematic forays into fantasy and science fiction with John Boorman’s take on the Arthur legend, 1981’s “Excalibur,” in which Stewart played Leondegrance, and director David Lynch’s 1984 adaptation of Frank Herbert’s “Dune,” in which he played Gurney Halleck, a top officer in the Atreides household who becomes the trusted lieutenant to Paul (Kyle MacLachlan).

Earlier, on British television, he starred in the 1975 BBC miniseries “North & South,” an adaptation of the Elizabeth Gaskell novel, and then played Sejanus on “I, Claudius.” In the BBC’s “Maybury” from 1981-83 he starred as a psychiatrist at a hospital.

Patrick Hewes Stewart was born in Mirfield, Yorkshire, acting as a youth with various amateur drama societies in the region and leaving school at 15. He held a job as a newspaper reporter but ultimately chose acting over journalism. He lost his hair at age 18.

Stewart began his acting career at Manchester’s Library Theatre, after which he became a member of the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1966.

The actor lent his voice to a number of videogames associated with the “Star Trek” and “X-Men” franchises.

He was thrice married, the first time to choreographer Sheila Falconer, the second to Wendy Neuss, a producer of “Star Trek: The Next Generation.”

Survivors include third wife Sunny Ozell, whom he married in a 2013 ceremony presided over by Ian McKellen, as well as a daughter, Sophie Stewart, and son, actor Daniel Stewart, both from his marriage to Falconer.

Donations may be made to Johns Hopkins Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center Fund and Alzheimer’s Foundation of America Caregiver Resources .

article_text:
The fall film festivals are not over. London is still underway, and AFI FEST kicks off in Los Angeles on October 21. And Thursday night launched this year’s Middleburg Film Festival, a four-day fest set at BET co-founder Sheila Johnson’s posh Salamander resort in the rolling hills of Virginia outside of Washington, D.C., which has grown into a formidable regional film festival, alongside upcoming events like SCAD and Virginia. Baseball-capped “ The Debut ” auteur Jesse Eisenberg was on my flight from New York; I filled him in on the virtues of a small awards -focused film festival.

Fest director Susan Koch is landing more and more top Oscar contenders and talent every year, as well as Oscar pundits to cover them. For the lucky attendees from the greater D.C. area, with just about 45 new features are on view, almost everyone gets into the venues. This year, the sell-outs include Eisenberg’s Telluride breakout “The Debut” (A24), Sundance hit “Wicker” (Black Bear), and TIFF crowdpleaser “I Play Rocky” (Amazon/MGM). If the press and talent guests are a select few, there’s more access to the folks roaming the halls. Indeed, Eisenberg held court in the Salamander lobby before heading into the screening and Q&A.

On opening night, I dropped into two festival receptions being held indoors due to rain. Koch thanked Amazon/MGM production executive Scott Foundas for luring some “I Play Rocky” talent to the festival. Searchlight distribution chief Derval Whelan is accompanying two auteurs, Martin McDonagh (“Wild Horse Nine”) and Tony Gilroy (“Behemoth!”). THR’s David Canfield and The Ankler’s Katey Rich debated the likely final five in the international feature race (Rich is rooting for German longshot “Everytime” ). Playing at the festival are the current frontrunners: Cannes prize-winners “Fatherland” and “Minotaur,” which may duke it out for the fifth slot, while Palme d’Or winner “Fjord,” director winner “La Bola Negra,” Cannes Actress-co-winner “All of a Sudden,” and Venice hit “Possible Love” are the likely top four.

Friday brings “The Invite” Oscar contender Seth Rogen In Conversation and the annual Women’s lunch; expected are Rosalind Eleazar, the breakout star of “Misty Green,” and “The Debut” Best Actress frontrunner Julianne Moore — who popped out of an elevator Friday night looking dazzling and introduced herself to me as “Julie” — as well as actress Léa Seydoux and director Marie Kreutzer ( Netflix ‘s Cannes breakout “Gentle Monster”).

On Saturday, I will moderate a panel with Middleburg producer-advisors Ron Yerxa and Albert Berger (“Little Miss Sunshine”) and Bill Pullman, who plays a juicy role opposite Anders Danielsen Lie in Berlin director-winner “Everybody Digs Bill Evans” (Cohen Media). My colleague Marcus Jones will moderate a music panel , including Eisenberg and Daniel Pemberton who, along with “La Bola Negra” star Guitarricadelafuente, will also perform, plus Middleburg perennial, annual Oscar songwriter hopeful Diane Warren (17 Oscar nominations, no wins), who is wandering the Salamander halls showing people her new song for “Maserati: The Brothers” on her iPhone.

My great disappointment: at one point, I was going to do an interview in the Stallion Barn (the community is particularly horse-obsessed). That would have been a first.
excerpt_original: Regional festivals, like the just-opened Middleburg Film Festival, attract top awards contenders — and the pundits who cover them.

article_text:
Disney+ suma nuevas temporadas, ficciones originales y especiales para toda la familia. Entre los destacados del mes aparecen Somos así, La emperatriz divorciada y el regreso de Percy Jackson.

Disney+ presentó sus estrenos de noviembre de 2026, con novedades para todos los gustos. La programación incluye la tercera temporada de Percy Jackson y los dioses del Olimpo , la ficción argentina Somos así, la serie de Nadie dice nada , nuevas entregas de Todo Vale y The Kardashians , además de producciones de Marvel, documentales y especiales familiares. Estos son los principales lanzamientos y las fechas para tener en cuenta.

Miércoles 4 de noviembre – La emperatriz divorciada

Basada en el exitoso webtoon de NAVER, la serie sigue a Navier, la querida emperatriz del Reino del Este, cuyo matrimonio con el emperador Sovieshu entra en crisis cuando él se enamora de Rashta, una esclava fugitiva. Ante la intención de su esposo de divorciarse, Navier acepta con una condición: poder casarse con Heinrey, príncipe heredero del Reino del Oeste. Una historia de amor, traición, poder y arrepentimiento que amenaza el destino de dos reinos. Luego del estreno, llegarán dos episodios nuevos cada miércoles.

Miércoles 4 de noviembre – Todo Vale, temporada 2

La comedia legal de Ryan Murphy regresa con las abogadas del estudio Grant, Ronson & Greene. En esta nueva entrega habrá más escándalos, secretos y conflictos personales, mientras nuevas alianzas ponen a prueba las amistades y una revelación amenaza el futuro del bufete. El elenco está encabezado por Kim Kardashian, Naomi Watts, Niecy Nash-Betts, Teyana Taylor, Matthew Noszka, Cauã Reymond, Sarah Paulson y Glenn Close. Los capítulos siguientes se estrenarán cada miércoles.

Martes 10 de noviembre – VisionQuest

Después de ser reiniciado y escapar de quienes buscaban convertirlo en un arma, Vision intenta encontrar un nuevo propósito mientras permanece oculto. Para lograrlo, consulta a distintas inteligencias artificiales de su programación, entre ellas F.R.I.D.A.Y., E.D.I.T.H., J.A.R.V.I.S. y Ultrón. Sin embargo, una recompensa por su captura lo obliga a huir junto a Thomas Shepard, un joven misterioso que podría estar relacionado con la reencarnación de su hijo. En el final de temporada, deberá enfrentar su propia naturaleza y descubrir la verdad sobre su compañero.

Miércoles 18 de noviembre – Somos así, la serie de Nadie dice nada

La primera ficción inspirada en el popular programa de streaming de LUZU TV sigue a un grupo de amigos que atraviesa una etapa en la que todo parece desmoronarse: trabajos inestables, vínculos que cambian, citas fallidas y secretos inesperados. Protagonizada por Nico Occhiato, Flor Jazmín Peña, Momi Giardina, Santi Talledo y Martín Garabal, la serie explora con humor las dificultades de crecer y encontrar el propio rumbo. También participan Oscar Martínez, Graciela Stefani, Maite Lanata, Sofi Morandi, Olivia Nuss, Andrés Gil, Juli Poggio y Marixa Balli, entre otras figuras.

El elenco de Breaking Bad despidió a RJ Mitte tras conocerse la causa de su muerte

Denzel Washington, Daisy Edgar-Jones y Robert Pattinson se unen en ‘The Take’, el nuevo thriller de Netflix: Mirá las primeras imágenes

Viernes 20 de noviembre – Percy Jackson y los dioses del Olimpo, temporada 3

La exitosa adaptación de la saga literaria de Rick Riordan llevará por primera vez a la pantalla La maldición del Titán , el tercer libro de la colección. En esta temporada, Percy deberá afrontar la desaparición de Annabeth y una nueva profecía del Oráculo de Delfos que podría determinar el futuro del Olimpo. Según el vaticinio, un semidiós hijo de uno de los Tres Grandes podría salvar a los dioses o provocar su caída, arriesgando también su propia vida. Después del estreno inicial, se lanzarán dos episodios cada viernes.

Sábado 21 de noviembre – Outlander: Blood of My Blood, temporada 2

La precuela de Outlander llega al final de su segunda temporada con nuevos desafíos para sus familias y parejas. Mientras el ejército jacobita se prepara para la batalla en las Tierras Altas de Escocia, los distintos clanes deberán decidir de qué lado estarán. La serie está protagonizada por Jeremy Irvine y Hermione Corfield, como los padres de Claire, y Jamie Roy y Harriet Slater, como los padres de Jamie Fraser.

Viernes 27 de noviembre – Mickey: mi pobre angelito

Mickey está listo para pasar la Navidad en casa, pero Minnie sorprende a sus amigos con entradas para celebrar las fiestas en un famoso palacio de hielo. En medio de los preparativos, Mickey y Pluto quedan accidentalmente solos. Mientras ambos intentan proteger su hogar de un mapache y una comadreja que quieren robarse su cena navideña, Minnie y el resto de la pandilla harán todo lo posible por regresar a tiempo.

Más estrenos de Disney+ durante noviembre

Además de los lanzamientos principales, la plataforma incorporará nuevas series, temporadas y episodios semanales.

La mentira perfecta: serie de Hulu, con todos sus episodios disponibles desde el viernes 30 de octubre.

Disney Jr. Ariel – La Sirenita: relatos de la bahía encantada del delfín: cortos originales de Disney que se estrenarán completos el miércoles 4 de noviembre.

Lobos de cerca con Bertie Gregory: especial de National Geographic que llegará el viernes 6 de noviembre.

Entre pasos: en busca de un sueño: serie de Hulu que finalizará su temporada el martes 10 de noviembre.

It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia, temporada 18: la nueva entrega de la serie de FX estará disponible completa desde el miércoles 11 de noviembre.

Bluey: el restaurante elegante: nuevos episodios disponibles desde el lunes 16 de noviembre.

Toda la verdad, temporada 2: la serie de FX llegará a su final de temporada el jueves 26 de noviembre.

Temporada de amor: la ficción original de Hulu sumará un episodio nuevo cada miércoles.

The Kardashians, temporada 8: la serie original de Hulu estrenará un episodio nuevo cada jueves.

Scrubs, temporada 2: la serie de ABC también incorporará nuevos episodios cada jueves.

Phony: la otra madre: esta serie de misterio sigue a un adolescente que despierta en el hospital después de un accidente automovilístico y descubre que su madre, su única figura parental y mejor amiga, parece haber sido reemplazada por una impostora. Protagonizada por Connie Britton y Sam Nivola, entre otros, tendrá un episodio nuevo cada martes.

Deportes de ESPN en noviembre

La programación deportiva de ESPN tendrá un mes cargado de acontecimientos internacionales. En fútbol, se disputarán las finales de la CONMEBOL Libertadores y la CONMEBOL Sudamericana, además de nuevas jornadas de la UEFA Champions League, Europa League y Conference League, junto con partidos de las principales ligas europeas, la UEFA Nations League y la Copa Potrero.

El automovilismo ofrecerá cuatro fechas de Fórmula 1, en México, Brasil, Las Vegas y Catar, además de nuevas carreras de MotoGP. También habrá boxeo internacional con ESPN Knockout, la final del URBA Top 14 y los Test Matches de Los Pumas frente a Irlanda, Italia y Francia. A esto se sumarán la NBA, la NFL, el Maratón de Nueva York, el 133.º Abierto Argentino de Polo y dos nuevas fechas del Premier Padel Tour.

Con esta programación, Disney+ y ESPN ofrecerán durante noviembre una combinación de series originales, regresos esperados, entretenimiento familiar y grandes eventos deportivos.

article_text:
Films and events

Journey

Perfect Road

By turns exhilarating and intimate, this documentary portrait charts nomadic cyclist Max Schnell’s attempt to complete an extreme journey through some of Europe’s highest mountain passes.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Directors Adam Bonke, Christian Bonke

With Max Schnell, Nina Ridder

Denmark 2026. 91min

Courtesy of Dogwoof

Languages English, German With some English subtitles

Introduction

Max has been living on his bike for the last decade, pursuing what he sees as the most perfect form of freedom. While he undertakes his most gruelling challenge to date, his relationship with his partner, Nina, makes him question his life priorities. Adam and Christian Bonke enjoyed extensive access to craft a nuanced character study that unfolds against the backdrop of breathtaking mountain vistas.

Laure Bonville

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

The Match

Few sporting contests loom as large in the public imagination as the dramatic 1986 World Cup Quarter Final between England and Argentina, as this documentary details.

The Story of Documentary Film (The 1990s)

This fascinating chapter from Mark Cousins’ epic essay on the history of documentary chronicles a decade of formal reinvention and mainstream success.

Carl Sagan: We Are Made of Star Stuff

This awe-inspiring documentary is a detailed and thought-provoking portrait of the astronomer and astrophysicist behind Cosmos and Contact.

Daily Newsletter

Remembering Ursula von Rydingsvard

The monumental sculptor dies at 84; plus, how an artist snuck his own work into The Met, and a dispute over watercolors of Roma victims of the Holocaust.

Tonight’s the night! If you haven’t gotten your tickets to Hyperallergic’s Halloween Party, you still have a few hours to RSVP (and cobble an art costume together — or maybe just tape a banana to your shirt?)

Today, we remember the tremendous legacy of Ursula von Rydingsvard, whose monumental, organic sculptures bear the heavy trace of loss and the ever-present possibility of life. Born in Germany to Polish and Ukrainian parents, the artist and her family moved among displacement camps for Polish refugees before immigrating to the United States in 1950. Working across mediums — most spectacularly cedar beams — she lived a life of art in deep harmony with the natural world.

The thread of memory also runs through Roma scholar Cristiana Grigore's must-read essay on the battle over watercolors by the late Holocaust survivor Dina Gottliebova Babbitt. As the artist’s family fights to recover Babbitt’s haunting paintings of Roma prisoners of Auschwitz, currently housed in the Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum, Grigore asks: “What would justice look like for them?”

— Valentina Di Liscia, senior editor

In Battle Over Auschwitz Watercolors, Roma Victims Are Getting Left Behind

The decades-long ownership dispute between the family of late Holocaust survivor Dina Gottliebova Babbitt and the Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum over seven watercolors depicting Roma prisoners is back in the news. That’s because the dispute culminated in a California lawsuit initiated by her daughters 17 years after their mother’s death.

Nicknamed the “Angel of Death,” Dr. Josef Mengele ordered Babbitt to portray the traits of Roma prisoners as part of his pseudo-scientific experiments to prove what he perceived as their racial inferiority. Under these extreme life-and-death circumstances, Babbitt created the watercolors to save her life as well as her mother’s. All the Roma people forced to pose for these portraits were later executed.

The news coverage and conversations around the ownership dispute have long missed an essential frame through which to view this tragedy: the rights and dignity of the Roma people who were depicted, killed, and forgotten. What decision would best honor them? How do we stop the harmful experiment’s long-term impact from further stigmatizing Roma identity? | Cristiana Grigore

Obituary

Ursula von Rydingsvard, Who Sculpted Monuments of Cedar, Dies at 84

Ursula von Rydingsvard, a sculptor whose monumental objects were partly inspired by her childhood in post-World War II refugee camps, died in her Manhattan home October 27, at 84.

During her over five-decade career, Von Rydingsvard chipped away at enormous cedar beams to create a menagerie of massive sculptures, from an assembly of cones to a 17-foot-tall tornado-shaped behemoth made from 15,000 pounds of wood. The abstract sculptor worked with an array of other materials, including bronze, textiles, and animal intestines. | Anna Lee

10 Art Shows to See in Los Angeles This November

The art community in Los Angeles is digging deep into history this November, excavating and reframing it through novel juxtapositions and archival findings.

Isabelle Frances McGuire tackles the Salem Witch Trials with a video game that bears uneasy relevance to our current age of creeping authoritarianism (just in time for next week’s midterms). Milano Chow draws on the archives of the LA Public Library to create ghostly architectural facades that seem at once familiar and foreign. At LACMA, an exhibition gives proper due to the city’s pioneering Brockman Gallery of 1967–90, which gave early support to scores of Black artists. And at the Brick, a retrospective brings together the two sides of Todd Gray’s long career: his commercial photos of musical acts and his post-modern tableaux, which themselves pull from archival images to construct new narratives. | Matt Stromberg

News

Tammy Nguyen Plumbs Nationhood and the Sea in New Opera

The artist will present an aria from the still-unfinished opera, “Timaeus and The Teacher,” during the closing program of the 61st Venice Biennale.

Timaeus and the Teacher at Wesleyan University (photo Elisabeth Bernstein, courtesy the artist and Lehmann Maupin)

Artist Tammy Nguyen will present the foreword to her debut opera Timaeus and The Teacher at the 61st Venice Biennale's closing program on November 13 and 14, capping off an eventful edition of the international contemporary art festival.

The aria is the entry point to Nguyen's still-unfinished opera, which traces the national and ideological impacts of the Vietnam War and fuses Plato’s theories of the cosmos with enduring questions of identity. Inspired by her father's experiences as a refugee aboard a vessel in the South China Sea, Nguyen centers the performance around a Vietnamese English teacher who attempts to flee Saigon (since renamed to Ho Chi Minh City) by boat, two years after North Vietnamese forces captured the capital in 1975. Grammy-nominated tenor Brian Vu will sing the libretto as the titular teacher, while a group of dancers will maneuver around him with a tapestry composed of flags.

“I was really fascinated by what happened at sea, as are many children of refugees from war-torn countries,” Nguyen told Hyperallergic in a phone interview. “The South China Sea is such a heavily trafficked area, and it created little stories where humans and the global economy collided.”

Commissioned and produced by Wesleyan University, where Nguyen teaches as an associate professor, the opera echoes themes prevalent in the artist’s other works , including a series of paintings on view at the biennale's Central Pavilion through November 22.

The tapestry of flags at the heart of the performance extends upon Nguyen's 2024 exhibition Timaeus and the Nations at the Sarasota Art Museum, where the artist rearranged 46 "flags of convenience," alluding to the practice in which ship operators change their flags for tax and regulation benefits.

Choreographed by Jamal Jackson, the opera's dancers will configure the tapestry into mountain ranges, a ship, the sea, and the cosmological diagram championed by the Pythagorean philosopher of Plato’s dialogue, Timaeus.

“Opera has a gestalt of sorts, just this massive tapestry of coming together and telling a story,” said Nguyen, adding that she's had the goal of directing an opera since learning to play and write music in San Francisco. “I took the anthems of all the countries in the flags of convenience, extracted various lyrics, and hybridized them arbitrarily for the libretto.”

As Vu’s character journeys across the sea, musical accompaniments mirror his literal and ideological movements. Nguyen assembled the libretto by breaking down traditional English language structures through a fractal sequence, while composer Neely Bruce remixed national anthems into the musical score.

Other performances slated for the final days of the biennale include a gathering around a Ouija board led by Hagar Ophir, stories of cultivation and global exchange with Lebanese artists Ziad Antar, Hatem Imam and Nayla Mabsout, and a meditation on salt as an essential mineral from Nathalie Vairac. While it’s unclear when the full production of the opera will be presented to audiences, Nguyen aims to have it completed by Bruce’s 85th birthday, in fall of 2029.

“The idea of nationhood is so flexible,” Nguyen stated. “But people die over it and fight over it, questioning whether they belong. We grapple with these questions all the time, as people who are looking to feel at home or develop a sense of agency for ourselves.”

article_text:
Die Kunst der Woche in Dresden, Frankfurt am Main, Hamburg, München, New York und Turin

Eröffnung des Casanova Museums in Dresden

Giacomo Casanova haftet bis heute vor allem der Ruf des legendären Liebhabers an. Eine neue Dauerausstellung in der Dresdner Altmarkt-Galerie will jetzt zeigen, dass Casanova weit mehr war als ein Verführer, und zugleich seine bislang wenig bekannte Verbindung zur Elbestadt beleuchten.

Diese Verbindung ist eng mit Casanovas Familie verknüpft: Seine Mutter und seine Geschwister lebten in Dresden und waren als Schauspieler, Maler und Tänzerin Teil des höfischen Kulturlebens. Die Stadt ist damit auch ein Schlüssel zu einer weniger bekannten Seite des Italieners. Auf zwei Etagen zeichnet das Casanova Museum sein bewegtes Leben nach. Rund 200 Exponate lassen die vergangene Epoche lebendig werden: Prächtige Gewänder, geheimnisvolle Masken, Gemälde, eine Kutsche und sogar eine venezianische Gondel gibt es zu sehen. Ein Nachbau jener Gefängniszelle, aus der Casanova einst aus den Bleikammern Venedigs entkam, erinnert an eine der berühmtesten Episoden seines Lebens.

Die Ausstellung setzt auf Entdeckerfreude statt auf stilles Betrachten. Hörstationen, mediale Installationen und Objekte zum Anfassen laden zum Mitmachen ein. Etwa bei einer Datingstation: Hier können Besucherinnen und Besucher herausfinden, ob Casanova auch heute noch ihr Typ wäre und ob sie dem berühmten Verführer wohl wie auf der Dating-App Tinder einen Swipe nach rechts geben würden. (dpa/Monopol)

Casanova Museum , Dresden, ab 31. Oktober

Rodin in Dresden

Mehrere Werke des französischen Bildhauers Auguste Rodin (1840-1917) kehren erstmals nach Jahrzehnten wieder zu ihrem angestammten Platz in den Staatlichen Kunstsammlungen Dresden (SKD) zurück. Unter dem Titel "Das große Drama. Auguste Rodin und der Streit um die Moderne" sind ab Samstag im Albertinum rund 70 Plastiken Rodins sowie anderer französischer und belgischer Künstler zu sehen, teilten die SKD mit.

In der Exposition treten sie in einen Dialog mit 24 Gemälden sowie Fotografien, Medaillen, Plaketten und historischen Dokumenten ein. Viele der Werke waren seit 1939 nicht mehr öffentlich zu sehen. "Die Ausstellung macht sichtbar, wie die Dresdner Sammlung zu einer der innovativsten und wichtigsten der europäischen Moderne wurde - und wie heftig um diese neue Kunst gestritten wurde", hieß es vom Albertinum. (dpa)

"Das große Drama. Auguste Rodin und der Streit um die Moderne", Albertinum , Dresden, bis 22. August 2027

Discovery Art Fair in Frankfurt am Main

Auf der Discovery Art Fair, in Köln und Frankfurt am Main zu Hause, sucht man nicht nach bekannten Namen, sondern kann neue Künstlerinnen und Künstler kennenlernen, die sich teilweise direkt an eigenen Messeständen vorstellen. Neben Emerging Artists finden sich auch ältere Künstlerinnen und Künstler, die vielleicht einem größeren Publikum noch nicht bekannt sind. Insgesamt 120 Aussteller aus rund 20 Ländern versammeln sich Ende Oktober in der Frankfurter Messe. Spannend sind die Förderkojen unter dem Motto " Discover a Talent", für die eine Jury besonders vielversprechende Künstlerinnen und Künstler aussucht. Auch der Kauf ist originell: Manche Werke können in einer Silent Auction erworben werden. Erst am letzten Messetag weiß man, wer den Zuschlag bekommt.

Discovery Art Fair , Frankfurt am Main, bis 1. November

Hito Steyerl in Hamburg

In ihren Videoessays, Installationen und Lecture Performances verwebt Hito Steyerl dokumentarische Fragmente mit fiktiven Elementen zu Narrativen, die sich mit globalen Machtstrukturen im digitalen Zeitalter auseinandersetzen. Mit rund 15 zwischen 1999 und 2025 entstandenen Rauminstallationen bietet eine Soloschau in den Hamburger Deichtorhallen einen breiten wie tiefgehenden Einblick in Steyerls Schaffen: Eine hybride Bildwelt, die algorithmische Kontrolle, Ausbeutung durch technologische Systeme, Kapitalismus, Klimakollaps und Krieg thematisiert, entfaltet sich über die gesamte Halle für aktuelle Kunst. Erstmals in Deutschland ist ihr neuester Film "The Island" zu sehen, der in mehrere Erzählungen eintauchen lässt, die durch das wiederkehrende Element der Überschwemmung miteinander verbunden sind.

Hito Steyerl: Deine Mudda macht Show" , Deichtorhallen, Hamburg, bis 29. März 2027

Freier Museumseintritt in Hamburg

Am morgigen Samstag, 31. Oktober, öffnen 50 Hamburger Museen ihre Türen. Unter dem Motto "#seeforfree" können am Reformationstag die teilnehmenden Häuser und Gedenkstätten besucht werden, wie die Kulturbehörde mitteilte. Viele Museen bieten demnach für diesen Tag ein Sonderprogramm mit Mitmach-Aktionen an.

Unter den 50 Museen und Gedenkstätten sind die Hamburger Kunsthalle, das Altonaer Museum und das Museum der Arbeit. Im Retro-Spiele-Club können Games auf Konsolen und Computern der letzten 50 Jahre gezockt werden. Das Deutsche Hafenmuseum macht etwa mit einem Schwimmkran und einer ausgestellten Barkasse die Geschichte der Hafenarbeit erlebbar. Außerdem werde es Vorführungen des Reepschläger-Handwerks, einen Shanty-Chor zum Mitsingen und einen Mini-Hyrox-Parcours geben, teilte die Kulturbehörde mit. Auch für Fußballfans ist etwas dabei: Das FC St. Pauli Museum und das HSV-Museum öffnen ihre Pforten. Auch Parabel – Zentrum für Kunst in Hamburg macht zum ersten Mal bei der Aktion mit. (dpa/Monopol)

"#seeforfree", verschiedene Museen, Hamburg, 31. Oktober

Gonzaldo Borondo in München

Der spanische Künstler Gonzalo Borondo wurde durch monumentale Wandarbeiten und Mixed-Media-Projekte bekannt. Er schafft visuelle Räume, die sich in einem ständigen Zustand der Transformation zu befinden scheinen. Borondos Ausstellung in der Münchener Villa Stuck bewegt sich zwischen Installation, Klangraum und begehbarer Bildmaschine. Der Ausstellungsparcours vereint klassische Märchen, antike Mythologie, barocke Ikonografie und elektronische Musik. Mit Spiegelräumen, Automaten, Klangobjekten und einem gläsernen Labyrinth erschafft Borondo eine Welt der Verwandlung und Lebendigkeit von Materie.

Gonzalo Borondo: "Mater", Museum Villa Stuck, München, bis 14. März 2027

Maria Jarema in München

Als "revolutionäre Kommissarin der Abstraktion" bezeichnete der Theatermacher Tadeusz Kantor die polnische Künstlerin Maria Jarema (1908–1958), deren Leben eng mit der Bühne verbunden war – unter anderem gründete sie in ihrer Heimatstadt Krakau eine Theatergruppe. Sie entwarf Kostüme und Bühnenbilder, war Schauspielerin, aber auch Bildhauerin, Malerin und experimentierfreudige Grafikerin. Als zentrale Künstlerin der polnischen Moderne wird Jarema in einer Schau am Münchener Lenbachhaus umfassend gewürdigt, unter anderem mit Gemälden, Monotypien, Skulpturen und Kostümen aus allen Schaffensphasen.

Maria Jarema: "Revolutionäre Kommissarin der Abstraktion" , Lenbachbaus, München, bis 25. April 2027

Roy Lichtenstein in New York

Als einer der prägenden Künstler der Pop-Art verwandelte Roy Lichtenstein (1923–1997) die Bildsprache der Massenkultur – Comics, Werbung oder Konsumgüter – in einige der bekanntesten Bilder des 20. Jahrhunderts. Die Bilder des New Yorkers wirken kühl, klar und maschinell gefertigt, sind aber handgemacht und zeigen einen Künstler, der fasziniert davon war, wie Bilder konstruiert, kopiert, vergrößert, verbreitet und neu erfunden werden.

Die Schau "Roy Lichtenstein: Like New" im New Yorker Whitney Museum bringt rund 130 Arbeiten zusammen, die von den frühen 1940er- bis in die 1990er-Jahre entstanden sind. Sie zeigt, wie Lichtensteins frühes Interesse an Wahrnehmung und visueller Erkennbarkeit eine lebenslange Auseinandersetzung mit Vervielfältigung, Simulation und Bildkultur prägte. Erstmals werden in der Ausstellung sämtliche Arbeiten aus Lichtensteins erster Pop-Art-Ausstellung in der Galerie Leo Castelli von 1962 wieder zusammengeführt.

Roy Lichtenstein: "Like New" , Whitney Museum, New York, bis 10. Mai 2027

Artissima in Turin

Lebe lieber ungewöhnlich, heißt es – selbst wenn das bedeutet, an einem Arm zu saugen, als wäre es ein frischer Apfel. " Sucker!" heißt dieses Bild der griechischen Malerin Amalia Vekri. Auf der 33. Artissima in Turin ist es im Programm der Una Galleria zu finden, die 2018 im italienischen Piacenza gegründet wurde – junge Kunst kann auch in der Peripherie gedeihen, so die Idee. Typisch Artissima: Die einzige Messe in Italien, die sich ganz der zeitgenössischen Kunst widmet, ist immer ein guter Ort für Experimente – und stellt die Kunst wirklich in den Fokus.

Von den 183 teilnehmenden Galerien, darunter Chert Lüdde aus Berlin, A Gentil Carioca aus Rio de Janeiro oder Continua aus San Gimignano, zeigt mehr als ein Drittel monografische Ausstellungen in ihren Kojen. Zahlreiche Preise, gesponsert von Illy, Seletti und anderen, stützen die Qualität des Angebots. Direktor Luigi Fassi versteht seine Messe als Ort des kulturellen Austauschs und findet, dass Kunst als öffentliche Intelligenz die demokratischen Institutionen einer Gemeinschaft stärken und bereichern könne. Er beschwört die Kraft der Imagination – was sowohl für die Emerging Artists in der kuratierten Sektion " Present Future" als auch für die Werke der 1930er- bis 1990er-Jahre in der Sektion " Back to the Future" passt.

Artissima , Turin, bis 1. November

article_text:
All exhibitors who participated in the most recent edition of Art Basel Paris, which closed two days early because of planned protests, will get a 20 percent reduction on their final invoices.

“We will exceptionally be extending a 20 percent reduction on booth fees to all galleries that participated in the Paris fair, in recognition of the closure,” on October 24–25, Art Basel chief executive Noah Horowitz told ARTnews in an interview.

Additionally, tickets purchased for that weekend have already been refunded. Galleries typically pay up front for most of their participation, but the final invoices come within 30 days of a fair’s closure, and they will reflect the new discount. The reduction will not apply to so-called “special orders” (lights, booth customisation, etc.), as the latter represent a third-party expense that Art Basel does not control. For example, if a gallery’s booth fee were $10,000, and the additional special order service fees accrued during the fair’s installation, such as lighting costs and any customization to the booth, were $10,000, for a total of $20,000, the exhibitor would receive a discount of $2,000.

Since Art Basel Paris announced it would shut early for security reasons ahead of a new wave of protests, participating exhibitors, particularly smaller and emerging galleries, have been eagerly awaiting to hear whether they will be compensated for the lost time.

The fair opened to its “Avant Première” preview to VVIP guests on Tuesday, October 20, with its Wednesday and Thursday openings also being exclusive to invited guests. The fair was only open to the public for one day, Friday, instead of extending to Saturday and Sunday as originally planned.

“[I’m] conscious that it’s taken about two and a half weeks to get here, but we wanted to bring this all together comprehensively and ensure that we engaged our gallery community properly before implementing and rolling all this out,” said Horowotiz.

Art Basel, which is in the midst of preparing its Miami Beach edition (running December 2–6), also sent a letter about the discount to all participating galleries Wednesday, signed by Art Basel Paris director Karim Crippa . “While we appreciate that the closure impacted galleries in different ways, we believe this approach offers a fair and considered way forward, reflecting our appreciation of the partnership we share and our commitment to strengthening it further,” it states.

The Letter

The news comes following a strongly worded letter from the French galleries association Comité Professionnel des Galeries d’Art (CPGA) addressed to Crippa, dated October 28, demanding “fair compensation” for the shortened event, as first reported by Monopol .

In its letter, the CPGA, which counts over 340 members and represents 57 of the 211 galleries who exhibited at Art Basel Paris, complained that the fair had shown “contempt” or “disregard” (the original French term used was “ mépris ”) for not consulting exhibitors before announcing the early closure.

There was “a lot of anger and incomprehension” about the extent of communication between the fair and its exhibitors on the discussion of when to close, according to one leading CPGA member speaking to ARTnews anonymously to protect their relationships. They added: “We understand it was a difficult decision to make, but we don’t understand why no one was consulted, not even for a few minutes!”

In an October 29 email update from the CPGA to its members, the group stated further: “Such a decision called for opening a dialogue with the exhibitors’ representatives; it was the subject of no prior discussion.”

The fair’s Saturday closure has been widely accepted as necessary because of protests scheduled that day, including one that called for people to gather outside the Grand Palais, the venue for Art Basel Paris. Many exhibitors, however, were surprised that the fair would not reopen on Sunday. Protests were not planned for that day, and a major Cezanne exhibition located in another part of the Grand Palais reopened Sunday.

“We fully support the Saturday closure. As a measure of precaution, it seemed to us absolutely essential after the security failure of the previous weekend and the extremely serious unrest that followed. But we would have liked to argue for reopening on Sunday,” CPGA president Philippe Charpentier told the Art Newspaper, France last month.

In response to the CPGA’s remonstrance, Horowitz told ARTnews : “This is a highly dynamic situation we were responding to. We had many conversations with many galleries during the fair and certainly in the weeks following, and I think we learned a lot of lessons coming through this. And as all businesses do, we’ll continue to improve our processes and make adjustments for the future.”

About staying closed through Sunday, he added that, “Given the uncertainty surrounding the potential impact and duration of the planned demonstrations, as well as access to the Grand Palais, we couldn’t be confident at the time that conditions would allow for a safe reopening on Sunday. Several exhibitors also expressed serious concerns about leaving the artworks in the Grand Palais unattended on the Saturday. In recognition of all of that, we concluded that closing early and beginning the dismantling on Friday evening was the most responsible course of action, and ultimately in the best interest of safeguarding the artworks themselves, but also the gallerists, teams, all the workers, and, of course, the visitors as well.”

Horowitz also confirmed a December 14 meeting is planned between Art Basel Paris and CPGA, to talk more broadly about the “overarching situation [and] the broader relationship” between various parties. Though Horowitz said such meetings regularly take place, the forthcoming one follows the CPGA’s specific request to convene with Art Basel leadership about redress for the shortened fair.

Representatives of France’s Ministry of Culture and the Grand Palais RMN venue are also expected to attend, but both told ARTnews they have not been involved with the question of discounts for the shortened fair. (Horowitz said he could not comment on Art Basel’s contract with the venue, French authorities, or its insurance arrangements.)

“Our role is to ensure a space for constructive dialogue: to understand the impact on the galleries, the organizer and the host venue, and to learn lessons from this situation,” a Culture Ministry spokesperson told ARTnews in a statement.

What the Dealers Say

The CPGA is not the only one that has formally requested compensation. ARTnews reached out to dozens of smaller galleries outside of France to ask how they think the fair handled the closure, whether they agree some reimbursement is in order (they all said yes), and if so, what kind. To the latter question, answers ranged from suggesting the fair prioritize reimbursements for smaller galleries to proposing the fair pay back one third of the booth fair price, since that was the amount of time the fair was cut short. Vouchers toward next year’s application and booth fees were also suggested.

Horowitz said that unlike some sort of credit scheme for future Art Basel fairs, “we thought the most important thing was to directly tie it to and provide immediate relief now for those that showed with us at the fair in October.”

“We felt that a 20 percent reduction was a fair and reasonable place to land,” he added. He also explained the fair has “concerns for the success of all galleries across all sectors of our fairs,” no matter their size or prominence.

Many of the dealers interviewed for this article said they trusted Art Basel had made the best decision, given the information they had at the time, in regard to the closure. They also said they agreed with CPGA’s demands and appreciated its lobbying on behalf of participating galleries. But the dealers often shied away from the harsher language used in the CPGA’s letter, including that exhibitors had been treated with “contempt.”

“We all feel that our interests are well-defended, and personally I feel like the French gallery association, and Philippe Charpentier from Mor Charpentier, [the CPGA’s president], will advocate for all of us, not just the French galleries. They are the best equipped to deal with it,” said Los Angeles– and New York–based dealer François Ghebaly. “Because of that letter [from the CPGA], we felt no need to press forward,” with further claims, he added.

The CPGA has also successfully led lobbying efforts in the past to the French government, notably on issues such as lowering art sales tax to 5.5 percent.

Ghebaly’s prominent mid-sized gallery did well at the fair, largely thanks to advanced planning, rather than relying on chance encounters to make key sales. “It was a pretty extreme and unprecedented situation, and in a way, I think [the fair] did okay,” Ghebaly said. “I’m glad most of the event was able to move forward as planned for the beginning of the week, and then they made a call, which I’m sure was a complicated decision.”

However, he said, “Conversations were a little different with younger dealers who are starting out and are upstairs in the alleys [of the Grand Palais]. They may have a loss of income that is more difficult to absorb.”

Though the fair reported selling 306 artworks for $148 million by Wednesday, much of that business was done by major galleries, who typically complete their sales after the first few days. Smaller and emerging galleries were hit hardest by the shortened schedule, because they rely on those final days to close deals. Visitors also tend to use the rest of the week to see booths along the venue’s periphery and upstairs level, while smaller-budgeted collectors from the region visit more affordable galleries over the weekend, when they’re off work.

Aron Gent, owner of Document, a gallery with spaces in Chicago and Lisbon, told ARTnews he formally requested a partial refund from Art Basel; His booth was located in the fair’s upstairs corridors.

“The closure affected us greatly, being 1/3 shorter, as we sell mostly works under [$]10k that a great deal of weekend attendees can afford,” Gent wrote in an email. “Also, most of the artists in our booth are unknown to a majority of the people who enter our booth, so the main goal is to educate them on their practices and hope for additional exhibition opportunities and the possibilities of future sales.”

He added that, on further reflection, the fair should have announced earlier, on Tuesday, that they would close early, and then extended daily opening hours for the remaining days, “to accommodate as many people as possible.”

Other dealers said they had also been waiting to hear about reimbursement, but felt they lacked the power to do much about it. Ellen de Bruijne, who runs the eponymous gallery in Amsterdam, said that being a small gallery from the Netherlands, she was “not in a position to demand” compensation from Art Basel Paris. An associate at LC Queisser, which has spaces in Tbilisi, Georgia, and Cologne, Germany, said the gallery is “simply waiting for Art Basel to come up with a proposed solution, whether that involves compensation or, for example, a reduction in the application fee. We are not requesting any specific form of compensation, but some form of compensation.”

The associate continued, “Even just considering hotel costs and staff who had already travelled to Paris, galleries have lost money. … We don’t necessarily think anything would have happened, but the public anticipation and concern were already so intense that many people decided not to come to Paris over the weekend. We think it was reasonable to take these precautions.”

Going forward, dealers observed that disturbances to large art-world gatherings on a similar scale may become the new normal. “We are living through a turbulent moment across the world,” said Ghebaly. “There may be more disruptions of these kinds of massive events, and we should get used to it.”

article_text:
The 67th Thessaloniki Intl. Film Festival, which runs from Nov. 5 to 15, has revealed the lineups of its Meet the Neighbors+ and >>Film Forward competition sections.

Among the films in the Meet the Neighbors+ section are Blerta Basholli, who won at Sundance with “Hive,” and comes to Thessaloniki with Kosovan War coming-of-age drama “Dua,” winner of the SACD Award at Critics’ Week in Cannes. Also competing is Myrsini Aristidou’s “Hold Onto Me,” winner of the Audience Award in the World Cinema – Dramatic section of Sundance Film Festival. The film was described in its Variety review as “a heartfelt drama” that “follows a plucky young girl smitten with her long-absent, scoundrel father.” Pierre Le Gall’s gay trucker love story “Flesh and Fuel,” which won best film at Zurich, is also competing.

'Matchbox: The Movie' Review: John Cena Can't Make This Toy-Car Spinoff Feel Grownup

The section consists of debut or sophomore films of upcoming film directors that “intend to offer us a deeper understanding on life, the human condition and the state of things in our wider geographical region or cast a glance at the world ‘beyond our neighborhood’ through a unique and innovative artistic prism,” the festival said.

Popular on Variety

The jury is composed of Cristina Cassano, head of Contemporary Italian Cinema Promotion at Cinecittà, filmmaker Sofia Exarchou and Anne Østerud, a film editor.

The films will compete for the Golden Alexander – Michel Dimopoulos Award, accompanied by a 10,000 euro ($11,240) cash prize, and the Silver Alexander for best direction, which comes with a 5,000 euro ($5,620) cash prize. The jury will also bestow the best actor and actress awards, and may also award a screenplay award or an artistic achievement award.

“Chronicles From the Siege,” Abdallah Al-Khatib, Algeria-France-Palestine “Dua,” Blerta Basholli, Kosovo-Switzerland-France “Flesh and Fuel,” Pierre Le Gall, France-Poland “Furies,” Rami Kodeih, Lebanon-Brazil “The Lost Son,” Darko Stante, Slovenia-Greece-Croatia-Italy-North Macedonia “Until the Day Ends,” Jelena Maksimović, Serbia-Bulgaria-Slovenia-Montenegro-Germany-Croatia “Where Giants Sleep,” Arthur Michel, Belgium-Kosovo (world premiere) “Elena’s Shift,” Stefanos Tsivopoulos, Greece “Recrucified,” Theo Papadoulakis, Greece-Italy-Luxembourg-Cyprus (European premiere) “Hold Onto Me,” Myrsini Aristidou, Cyprus-Greece-Denmark “The Lion at My Back,” Tonia Mishiali, Cyprus-Luxembourg-Greece

The films are competing for the Golden Alexander >>Film Forward – Best Feature Film Award, accompanied by a 10,000 euro cash prize, the Silver Alexander – Best Direction Award, accompanied by a 5,000 euro cash prize, and the best actor and actress awards. The jury may also award a best screenplay award or a best artistic achievement award.

“Chronovisor,” Jack Auen, Kevin Walker, U.S. “Filipiñana,” Rafael Manuel, Singapore-U.K.-Philippines-France-the Netherlands “I Plant My Hand in the Garden,” Boris Hadžija, Hoda Taheri, Germany-Serbia-U.S. “Objet A,” Ann Oren, Germany-Luxembourg-Greece “Ponderosa,” Rob Rice, U.S. “Promised Spaces,” Ivan Marković, France-Germany-Cambodia-Serbia “Snapshot,” Joseph Archer, U.K. “The Golden Age,” Bérenger Thouin, France-Italy “Particles of Dust,” Argyris Germanidis, Greece-Germany (world premiere) “Under the Judas Tree,” Christos Manson Chouliaras, Greece-Cyprus

article_text:
The artist duo Brognon Rollin has been awarded the 2026 Prix Marcel Duchamp.

David Brognon and Stéphanie Rollin were selected from a shortlist of four artists including Joël Andrianomearisoa, Laura Henno and Josèfa Ntjam . The duo will receivea €35,000 prize on top of the €10,000 awarded to each shortlisted artist to assist with the development of their shortlist exhibition.

David Brognon, born in Belgium in 1978, and Stéphanie Rollin, born in Luxembourg in 1980, work between Paris, Siena and Luxembourg, began collaborating in 2006. Their work encompasses installations, video, performance and conceptual interventions, such as their work included in the Prix Duchamp exhibition, One Hour at a Time (2026), an amusement park arcade coin-pushing machine, filled with tokens that are awarded to addicts and substance abusers for enduring points of sobriety and abstinence.

An exhibition of the prize’s shortlisted artists is on view at the Musée d’Art Moderne de Paris through 7 February 2027.

Open Studios

Sunset Park, Where You Can Still Get an Artist Studio for Under $600

At the Brooklyn neighborhood's Open Studios festival, artists showed off the works they make in converted factories, warehouses, and three-story walk-ups

Hyperallergic )

Lizzy Plapinger had barely settled into her studio in a sunny corner of Industry City before visitors spilled into the space on Sunday, October 18, to see a handful of her brightly contrasting geometric paintings laid against her walls for Sunset Park Open Studios .

“I just moved in two months ago from Bushwick, and I’m still getting to know the area, but it feels very welcoming,” Plapinger told Hyperallergic . “I like that it’s close to other artists and designers, which makes it feel ripe for collaboration.”

When New York artists needed a place to work after being priced out of their communities over the past decade, Sunset Park became one of their last refuges for affordable studio space. Known as an industrial manufacturing hub and enclave for Mexican and Chinese immigrants, the southwest Brooklyn neighborhood has drawn enough artists and creative workers to its converted factories, warehouses, and three-story walk-ups to sustain a three-day arts festival featuring more than 300 spaces.

Transient City exhibition at Court Tree Collective

title_original: A New Met Show Promises Rembrandt, as Never Seen Before
editorial_title_zh: 大都会艺术博物馆新展呈现前所未见的伦勃朗
editorial_excerpt_zh: 与卢浮宫共同策划的“伦勃朗与古代艺术”将首次把这位艺术家的多件作品带到美国。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "重新审视荷兰黄金时代最伟大的艺术巨匠之一伦勃朗，绝非易事。大都会艺术博物馆似乎正准备实现这一目标，其将于明年举办的一场展览将首次把这位艺术家的多件作品带到美国。", "links": [{"text": "Metropolitan Museum of Art", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/metropolitan-museum-of-art/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“伦勃朗与古代艺术”（Rembrandt and the Ancients）与卢浮宫博物馆合作举办，将于2027年11月在纽约开幕，该展被宣传为首个深入探讨该艺术家对地中海古代艺术与神话之迷恋的博物馆专题研究。这也将是大都会20年来首个专门纪念伦勃朗的大型展览，并将标志着至少三幅画作的美国首秀：《手持大卫王信件的拔示巴》、《巴达维亚人的宣誓》以及《浴于溪流中的女人》。这些作品将与来自40多家机构的120多幅绘画、版画和素描汇聚一展，大都会首席执行官兼馆长马克·霍莱因（Max Hollein）称其为“史无前例且充满力量的组合，展现了伦勃朗视野的深度”。该展览将于2027年11月至2028年2月28日在纽约展出，之后将巡展至卢浮宫。", "links": [{"text": "Louvre Museum", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/louvre-museum/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "该展览由大都会欧洲素描与版画策展人乔安娜·希尔斯·赛登斯坦（Joanna Sheers Seidenstein）与负责卢浮宫荷兰及佛兰德斯绘画的布莱兹·杜科斯（Blaise Ducos）共同策划。大都会将从其丰富的伦勃朗馆藏中借出4幅油画、3幅素描和11幅版画——其中包括已在56年前最后一次外借的《亚里士多德与荷马半身像》——而卢浮宫则将贡献2幅油画和2幅素描。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Rembrandt_Bathsheba-Holding-King-Davids-Letter.jpg?w=400", "alt": "《沐浴的拔示巴》。1654年。布面油画，142 x 142 cm。馆藏编号：MI957。摄影：Mathieu Rabeau。", "caption": "《沐浴的拔示巴》，作于1654年。巴黎卢浮宫博物馆，通过纽约大都会艺术博物馆；摄影：Mathieu Rabeau/RMN-GP", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在卢浮宫的出借作品中，包括创作于1654年的《手持大卫王信件的拔示巴》，画中描绘了这位女主人公紧紧抓住大卫王那封灾难性召集令的情景。伦勃朗极其精彩地呈现了她的心理动荡：拔示巴裸露的形体仿佛在昏暗的房间里散发着自身的光芒，宛如命运本身正在逼近。这幅画将与一件借自罗马国家博物馆的古代浮雕一同展出，据报道伦勃朗是通过复制品接触到这件浮雕的，正是它启发了他对由侍女服侍的拔示巴的描绘。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "与此同时，瑞典皇家美术学院将首次向美国出借其具有纪念碑意义的作品《巴达维亚人的宣誓》（约作于1661年）。该画官方正名为《克劳狄乌斯·西维利斯的阴谋》，描绘了塔西陀的《历史》中记载的一个情节：这位独眼的巴达维亚首领率同胞宣誓在公元69至70年反抗罗马帝国，并以宝剑封盟。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "赛登斯坦在声明中表示：“伦勃朗对古代的介入采取了广泛且极其、甚至狂野的创造性形式。尽管今天这位艺术家与传统紧密相连——堪称古典大师——但在当时，他的作品却极为新鲜——在自然主义和情感即时性上展现出人性化、能引发共鸣甚至原始的力量。他从不满足于顺理成章，而是借用古代主题来突破界限——无论是艺术上的还是社会上的。”", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Reframing Rembrandt, one of the Dutch Golden Age’s greats, is no small feat. The Metropolitan Museum of Art seems poised to pull it off, with an exhibition next year that will bring several of the artist’s works to the United States for the first time.

“Rembrandt and the Ancients,” organized with the Louvre Museum and opening in New York in November 2027, is billed as the first in-depth museum examination of the artist’s fascination with the art and mythology of Mediterranean antiquity. It will also be the Met’s first major exhibition dedicated to Rembrandt in 20 years and will mark the US debut of at least three paintings: Bathsheba Holding King David’s Letter , Oath of the Batavians , and Woman Bathing in a Stream . The works will join more than 120 paintings, prints, and drawings from more than 40 institutions in what Met CEO and director Max Hollein calls “an unprecedented and powerful ensemble that reveals the depth of Rembrandt’s vision.” The show will be on view in New York from November 2027 through February 28, 2028, after which it will travel to the Louvre.

The exhibition is co-organized by Joanna Sheers Seidenstein, the Met’s curator of European drawings and prints, and Blaise Ducos, who oversees Dutch and Flemish paintings at the Louvre. The Met will draw on its extensive Rembrandt holdings for four paintings, three drawings, and 11 prints—including Aristotle With a Bust of Homer , which was last loaned over 56 years ago—while the Louvre will contribute two paintings and two drawings.

Among the Louvre’s loans is Bathsheba Holding King David’s Letter , from 1654, which depicts the heroine grasping King David’s disastrous summons. Rembrandt renders her psychological turmoil spectacularly: Bathsheba’s nude form seems to emit its own light in the darkened room, as if fate itself were closing in. The painting will be displayed alongside an ancient relief borrowed from the National Roman Museum, reportedly introduced to Rembrandt through a reproduction, that inspired his depiction of Bathsheba attended to by a footmaid.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Fine Arts, meanwhile, will loan the monumental Oath of the Batavians (ca. 1661) to the US for the first time. Officially titled The Conspiracy of Claudius Civilis , the painting depicts an episode recounted in Tacitus’s Histories : the one-eyed Batavian chieftain swearing his compatriots to a rebellion against the Roman Empire in 69–70 CE, sealing their vows with a sword.

“Rembrandt’s engagement with antiquity took wide-ranging and extraordinarily, even wildly creative, forms. Although today this artist is so strongly associated with tradition—the consummate Old Master—his work was, in its moment, remarkably fresh—human, relatable, even raw in its naturalism and emotional immediacy,” Seidenstein said in a statement. “Never one to be satisfied with the expected, he deployed ancient themes to push boundaries—both artistic and social.”
