title_original: Sandra Wollner’s ‘Everytime’ Is a Stunning Film About Grief Like You’ve Never Seen Before
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/image-5.png?w=149", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Few human emotions are as fathomable as grief. Someone (or something) was here, had meaning and value and presence, and is now gone. There is a hole, a gap, an empty space. The pain that accompanies that void may manifest in different people in different ways, but its very existence is understandable. What makes people happy? What makes them sad? What makes them angry? Grief, well, that’s an easier question with a tougher answer."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For her third feature film , German filmmaker Sandra Wollner tackles the most tangible of dramatic genres — the grief tale — and turns it on its head in a way that our own David Ehrlich called “infinitely beguiling.” Mostly, the film shows how infinitely elastic and malleable this genre is, and the emotions that power it.", "links": [{"text": "film", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/film/"}, {"text": "Sandra Wollner", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/sandra-wollner/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/GodzillaMinusZero.jpg?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "Godzilla Minus Zero", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/GettyImages-2303762870_aeffe5.jpg?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "Los Angeles Mayor-elect Nithya Raman arrives at an event on November 5, 2026 in Los Angeles, California", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The logline for the Un Certain Regard winner is simple enough: after the death of teenager Jessie (Carla Hüttermann), her mother Ella (Birgit Minichmayr), her little sister Melli (Lotte Shirin Keiling), and her boyfriend Lux (Tristán López) form an unlikely family unit as they attempt to move on. To say much else is spoiler-y in the truest of senses: It would detract from the joy and wonder of watching this story unfold.", "links": [{"text": "Un Certain Regard winner", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/awards/results/cannes-film-festival-2026-award-winners-full-list-1235196021/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "That Wollner’s film is doing something different with seemingly well-trod material is obvious from the start, as “ Everytime ” layers on cut scenes from the video game “Vintage Story” — not “Minecraft,” though Wollner understands why the audience might think it’s the more well-known game — long before the real drama kicks in.", "links": [{"text": "That Wollner’s film is doing something different", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/news/trailers/everytime-trailer-sandra-wollner-cannes-winner-1235224540/"}, {"text": "Everytime", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/everytime/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A familiarity with “Vintage Story” is not required to understand her film, Wollner promised during a recent interview with IndieWire. “Maybe if someone hears the dialogue of Melli and Lux, then maybe they would feel they have to know more about it, because they’re talking about how you can basically cut trees to harvest stuff and to get that, but I don’t feel that you have to know anything,” she said."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Wollner herself isn’t even a “hardcore gamer,” but she admires video games for their world-building and how they can encourage exploration. Her early forays into both “Vintage Story” and “Minecraft” tickled that. “It felt like the ‘Backrooms’ phenomenon, but before the ‘Backrooms’ phenomenon,” she said. “You’re walking through infinite worlds that feel so big, but minimalistic in a way. And the sounds; a very ambient sound feels eerie and soothing at the same time. I was just very compelled and inspired by that.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The idea that Jessie would leave behind her own video game world that Melli could then play in was one of the film’s first seeds. “I thought, it’s a way of a memorial I haven’t seen so far,” she said. “[We have this] whole world of avatars and gaming communities where people meet online and then if someone really goes out, their avatar might live forever in there and create a life on its own in a way. I just found that very intriguing, and this is why I wanted in there.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/ccElsaOkazaki_EVERYTIME_240717_makingof_DSCF5556_Berlin.jpg?w=650", "alt": "", "caption": "Sandra Wollner on the set of ‘Everytime’ Elsa Okazaki", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "While the film is unique in how it handles digital mementos — avatars, literally — Wollner also pays close attention to real-world details that can make grief feel even bigger."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“One of the first scenes [I thought of] was Ella lying down on the couch and hearing how her daughter would come back [into their apartment],” the filmmaker said. “It’s something I think also everybody can relate to, even with a more natural loss and not such a tragic one. For example, when I was a kid, my aunt would always run down the stairs [in the apartment complex where we lived], and I would always hear her in the morning, running down in the morning. The noise was very specific to this person. I didn’t want it to be full on, but to let us think, it couldn’t be Jessie .”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Wollner was also intrigued early on by the “constellation of people” impacted by the loss of one. “The boy, the little girl, and the mother, it’s people I’ve met in my life in several decades, I would say, variations of them, but somehow similar constellations,” she said. “They seemed very clear to me. Three people who, especially the mother and the boy, really tried to do the right thing in a way. But there is a big conflict in there. They are having a weird dependent relationship. She needs him to grieve. He needs her to forgive. Of course, I could have made this conflict much bigger, but I really was interested in ordinary people who just try to do the right thing and just try to go along with that.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Having her own child added a new dimension to the film, even for Wollner. The filmmaker was editing the film when her daughter was born (her longtime partner is writer and cinematographer Timm Kröger, who also worked on the digital imaging in “Everytime”), an experience that deepened her understanding of her own work."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In the film’s second half, the trio travel to Tenerife, Spain on holiday, a place that baby Jessie (who we’ve seen in home videos) once visited. There, they discover another baby, who looks just like Jessie, playing happily in the same quiet space that baby Jessie once occupied."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“We watched the scene again of baby Jessie sitting there, and we looked at each other,” she said. “I always understood what [that scene] means for me, but there, we really felt it for the first time, being a parent. And I felt, oh, I really nailed it! I mean, that sounds so stupid, but when I had the baby, I think, as many people feel, you still sometimes have the feeling, oh, where does it come from? It’s suddenly here. Suddenly there’s a person there. It’s like with that moment when she walks around the corner, and baby’s sitting there.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Wollner was also compelled by the way we memorize different places and the unpredictability of memory. The odd little space, located in the far reaches of the resort’s clubhouse, comes to haunt Ella, Melli, and Lux in different ways, forever linked to Jessie and her absence."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“When my dad died, I was with him, and I suddenly had this image of him standing somewhere in this bend on the river and fishing, and it felt so familiar,” the filmmaker said. “This memory intruded on my present. We cannot control when we get a memory. They’re just coming. Sometimes we can make them happen to come. But we never know if maybe the weird place where we saw our baby sitting or the weird moment is the one that haunts us the most. It’s this weird banal little room with this weird banal kitschy toy that is playing this music. And this is the thing that then comes back.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Those “banal little” details pack immense emotional power. So do turns from Minichmayr and López, who never turn to over-the-top histrionics to convey their grief. Wollner’s choice to set the majority of the film a year after Jessie’s death helped, giving the characters some distance from the immediate stab of loss."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Everytime_MainStillTheBarricadesPanamaFilm_GregoryOke.jpg?w=650", "alt": "Everytime", "caption": "‘Everytime’ 1-2 Special", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“It was a conscious choice to pick some time after the death [to mostly focus the film on],” she said. “As a writer, we need to know what happened in the time between, and so I wrote that as well, but it honestly felt not depictable. I feel I can only fail to show that. I wasn’t interested in these big emotions. That just felt too overwhelming. And sometimes we are made to believe that grief comes in these neat boxes to check: Now you’re sad, now you’re angry, now you accept. Maybe you can be angry again, then you accept. It’s just this messy thing that you can feel for a very long time.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Keiling also offers a nuanced performance, built more on a kid’s curiosity than on saddling the young actress with big, showy scenes. There’s no screaming and crying here, no sobbing or yelling. But that doesn’t mean that Keiling wasn’t accessing some major emotions."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“I love to work with kids,” Wollner said. “And even having a kid, I think I still am a kid in a way. For this one, I met Lotte, I had not met another kid, I only met her, I did not do any other castings. article_text:
Few human emotions are as fathomable as grief. Someone (or something) was here, had meaning and value and presence, and is now gone. There is a hole, a gap, an empty space. The pain that accompanies that void may manifest in different people in different ways, but its very existence is understandable. What makes people happy? What makes them sad? What makes them angry? Grief, well, that’s an easier question with a tougher answer.

For her third feature film , German filmmaker Sandra Wollner tackles the most tangible of dramatic genres — the grief tale — and turns it on its head in a way that our own David Ehrlich called “infinitely beguiling.” Mostly, the film shows how infinitely elastic and malleable this genre is, and the emotions that power it.

The logline for the Un Certain Regard winner is simple enough: after the death of teenager Jessie (Carla Hüttermann), her mother Ella (Birgit Minichmayr), her little sister Melli (Lotte Shirin Keiling), and her boyfriend Lux (Tristán López) form an unlikely family unit as they attempt to move on. To say much else is spoiler-y in the truest of senses: It would detract from the joy and wonder of watching this story unfold.

That Wollner’s film is doing something different with seemingly well-trod material is obvious from the start, as “ Everytime ” layers on cut scenes from the video game “Vintage Story” — not “Minecraft,” though Wollner understands why the audience might think it’s the more well-known game — long before the real drama kicks in.

A familiarity with “Vintage Story” is not required to understand her film, Wollner promised during a recent interview with IndieWire. “Maybe if someone hears the dialogue of Melli and Lux, then maybe they would feel they have to know more about it, because they’re talking about how you can basically cut trees to harvest stuff and to get that, but I don’t feel that you have to know anything,” she said.

Wollner herself isn’t even a “hardcore gamer,” but she admires video games for their world-building and how they can encourage exploration. Her early forays into both “Vintage Story” and “Minecraft” tickled that. “It felt like the ‘Backrooms’ phenomenon, but before the ‘Backrooms’ phenomenon,” she said. “You’re walking through infinite worlds that feel so big, but minimalistic in a way. And the sounds; a very ambient sound feels eerie and soothing at the same time. I was just very compelled and inspired by that.”

The idea that Jessie would leave behind her own video game world that Melli could then play in was one of the film’s first seeds. “I thought, it’s a way of a memorial I haven’t seen so far,” she said. “[We have this] whole world of avatars and gaming communities where people meet online and then if someone really goes out, their avatar might live forever in there and create a life on its own in a way. I just found that very intriguing, and this is why I wanted in there.”

While the film is unique in how it handles digital mementos — avatars, literally — Wollner also pays close attention to real-world details that can make grief feel even bigger.

“One of the first scenes [I thought of] was Ella lying down on the couch and hearing how her daughter would come back [into their apartment],” the filmmaker said. “It’s something I think also everybody can relate to, even with a more natural loss and not such a tragic one. For example, when I was a kid, my aunt would always run down the stairs [in the apartment complex where we lived], and I would always hear her in the morning, running down in the morning. The noise was very specific to this person. I didn’t want it to be full on, but to let us think, it couldn’t be Jessie .”

Wollner was also intrigued early on by the “constellation of people” impacted by the loss of one. “The boy, the little girl, and the mother, it’s people I’ve met in my life in several decades, I would say, variations of them, but somehow similar constellations,” she said. “They seemed very clear to me. Three people who, especially the mother and the boy, really tried to do the right thing in a way. But there is a big conflict in there. They are having a weird dependent relationship. She needs him to grieve. He needs her to forgive. Of course, I could have made this conflict much bigger, but I really was interested in ordinary people who just try to do the right thing and just try to go along with that.”

Having her own child added a new dimension to the film, even for Wollner. The filmmaker was editing the film when her daughter was born (her longtime partner is writer and cinematographer Timm Kröger, who also worked on the digital imaging in “Everytime”), an experience that deepened her understanding of her own work.

In the film’s second half, the trio travel to Tenerife, Spain on holiday, a place that baby Jessie (who we’ve seen in home videos) once visited. There, they discover another baby, who looks just like Jessie, playing happily in the same quiet space that baby Jessie once occupied.

“We watched the scene again of baby Jessie sitting there, and we looked at each other,” she said. “I always understood what [that scene] means for me, but there, we really felt it for the first time, being a parent. And I felt, oh, I really nailed it! I mean, that sounds so stupid, but when I had the baby, I think, as many people feel, you still sometimes have the feeling, oh, where does it come from? It’s suddenly here. Suddenly there’s a person there. It’s like with that moment when she walks around the corner, and baby’s sitting there.”

Wollner was also compelled by the way we memorize different places and the unpredictability of memory. The odd little space, located in the far reaches of the resort’s clubhouse, comes to haunt Ella, Melli, and Lux in different ways, forever linked to Jessie and her absence.

“When my dad died, I was with him, and I suddenly had this image of him standing somewhere in this bend on the river and fishing, and it felt so familiar,” the filmmaker said. “This memory intruded on my present. We cannot control when we get a memory. They’re just coming. Sometimes we can make them happen to come. But we never know if maybe the weird place where we saw our baby sitting or the weird moment is the one that haunts us the most. It’s this weird banal little room with this weird banal kitschy toy that is playing this music. And this is the thing that then comes back.”

Those “banal little” details pack immense emotional power. So do turns from Minichmayr and López, who never turn to over-the-top histrionics to convey their grief. Wollner’s choice to set the majority of the film a year after Jessie’s death helped, giving the characters some distance from the immediate stab of loss.

“It was a conscious choice to pick some time after the death [to mostly focus the film on],” she said. “As a writer, we need to know what happened in the time between, and so I wrote that as well, but it honestly felt not depictable. I feel I can only fail to show that. I wasn’t interested in these big emotions. That just felt too overwhelming. And sometimes we are made to believe that grief comes in these neat boxes to check: Now you’re sad, now you’re angry, now you accept. Maybe you can be angry again, then you accept. It’s just this messy thing that you can feel for a very long time.”

Keiling also offers a nuanced performance, built more on a kid’s curiosity than on saddling the young actress with big, showy scenes. There’s no screaming and crying here, no sobbing or yelling. But that doesn’t mean that Keiling wasn’t accessing some major emotions.

“I love to work with kids,” Wollner said. “And even having a kid, I think I still am a kid in a way. For this one, I met Lotte, I had not met another kid, I only met her, I did not do any other castings. I just fell in love and thought, oh, she’s exactly what I thought of Melli could be and even better, so I trusted the script to her.”

Wollner worked with fellow filmmaker Juli Neuhaus, who served as a “kids’ coach” for the younger members of the cast. Wollner and Neuhaus were eager to meet Keiling where she was. The young performer loves to draw, so she would draw the scenes before performing them, to better understand what they were about, which allowed her to access a full spectrum of feeling.

“With Melli, there was no scene where she really had to act her grief,” she said. “I always felt that the film itself, the editing and the framing, the absence, we see her doing her homework, and then we see the same room behind her, but now we know that the sister is not there anymore, I always felt that this will tell us the grief, so she doesn’t need to act it. If she holds her phone and is texting her sister, it will already make us feel the grief. She doesn’t need to feel the heavy weight of that. So, actually for her, it was, I would say, like a very light shoot. Playful. It was really playful.”

Still, for all its sense of fantasy and play, “Everytime” is about a terrible heartbreak. Yet, as ever, Wollner chose to depict Jessie’s sudden, shocking death in a unique way, tracking her fall from a tall building while out with Lux from a great distance away. We can see it. We can do nothing about it. That’s grief, too.

“This was one that really was clear to me in the writing process already, that we’re going to have this lens and that we have this weird perspective of the universe itself looking at it, being so far away and still not able to do something about it, but still witnessing so intimate,” she said.

The actors were on one high-rise building, while Wollner and her crew were on another, about half a mile away. “And we had this insane lens. I had a 3,000-millimeter consumer camera, which is an insane lens,” she said. “It’s really like you don’t want to point it on people. It feels really not OK. But I was sure that I wanted to work with exactly that length or something similar to that, that feels kind of forbidden to be so close and too far away at the same time.”

While the scene is shot as if Jessie and Lux are very close to the edge of the building, the actors were not. (Hüttermann later told Wollner that she still had the feeling she might fall, even with myriad safety measures in place. That’s just how immersive the entire thing felt.) Hüttermann’s actual fall was shot in a studio, and their visual effects supervisor Kariem Saleh combined that footage with the outdoor shots.

Because they needed a certain kind of light, Wollner estimated they had only about five takes to get it right, though she knew they would likely only get one shot with the “perfect” light. Her script also called for the camera to follow a bird after the fall, but she said with a laugh, “Unfortunately, no bird came in exactly that moment.” (They lensed other birds, though, and those also ended up in the final composite shot.)

“We worked so many hours just on the sounds, just to get the right level of there is a little sound, and there is a little tink when she falls down, a little bit,” she said. “Just to realize, given how far away we had to be, how does the sound have to be? We worked the whole time on that, and I never really felt it until I sat at Cannes in the audience. And I heard the gasps for the first time and really it went through my bones. I mean, it’s weird to say that, but I was happy, but I felt the first time that it actually worked.”

Wollner remains very emotionally connected to the film, constantly talking about the way certain scenes make her feel , either while making them or editing them or even seeing them with an audience. Of course, such a deep-feeling filmmaker crafted such a beguiling film, one that invites all sorts of responses and theories. Since Cannes, audiences have been talking about its genuinely thrilling third act and the implications of its final scenes. And while we won’t spoil them here, we had to ask: What did Wollner want her viewers to feel in those moments?

“The feeling that I wanted to have is that [this film that is] grounded or hopefully grounded in the beginning, then suddenly you walk around the corner and you feel still some ground, but it’s such an odd place now and you don’t know,” she said. “I always hoped it doesn’t feel just dreamy, but there is some groundedness to it and that the people still react in a way that made sense for them, the characters, but that you don’t know what room you entered now, some kind of back room. That was clear from the beginning.”

And, as fantastical as it might sound, she’s clear: it’s all real. “I mean, it’s such a cliché to say that, but everything we see at the end is true at the same time,” she said.

A 1-2 Special release, the film is in limited theaters now, with a wide release to come in February 2027.
excerpt_original: The German filmmaker's portrait of life after tragedy is filled with the unexpected. She tells IndieWire about video game cut scenes, the power of banal memories, the scene that makes everyone gasp, and what it all means. Sort of.

The Indian contemporary art market has been on an upswing in recent years. The growth has been catalyzed by the country’s economic boom and explosion in private wealth. This has been amplified by a surge in prices for the work of India’s modern masters, now nearly inaccessible for emerging collectors. Galleries have been in rapid expansion mode, participating in more art fairs internationally, and opening new spaces.

Below is a primer looking at eight of India’s top galleries, whose programs are influential and at times cutting-edge. Listed alphabetically, the featured galleries regularly participate in leading international art fairs, have placed the work of their artists in major institutions, or represent artists who frequently appear on the biennial circuit.

A third generation is also involved in the gallery: Gandhy’s daughter, Atyaan Jungalwala, runs the offshoot space Chemould CoLab, which represents artists like Jayeeta Chatterjee and Gurjeet Singh. Address: 3rd floor, Queens Mansion, Ghanshyam Talwatkar Marg, Azad Maidan, Fort, Mumbai, Maharashtra 400001, India

Experimenter, Kolkata and Mumbai Image Credit: Vivienne Sarky/Courtesy Experimenter Founded by Prateek and Priyanka Raja in 2009, Experimenter quickly built a reputation for supporting alternative artistic practices often focused on photography and film, mixed media, and found objects. While Kolkata is often disconnected from art market hubs like Mumbai and Delhi, the gallery has approached that situation through an aggressive presence at leading art fairs, like Art Basel in Basel and Hong Kong, Frieze London New York, and FIAC in Paris. Prateek currently sits on the selection committee for Art Basel in Basel, Switzerland, while Priyanka does the same at Art Dubai. In 2018, it opened a second space in Kolkata and then in 2022 expanded to Mumbai. In 2025, they added a third outpost in Kolkata, inside the historical, colonial-era Alipore Jail, which has been renovated and repurposed as a cultural space. They have also organised a Curator’s Hub since 2010 which has drawn top curators like Doryun Chong, Hans Ulrich Obrist, Adam Szymczyk, and Naomi Beckwith. The roster includes a diverse range of South Asian and diaspora voices like Naeem Mohamien, Sanchayan Ghosh, Sakshi Gupta, Prabhakar Pachpute, Pushpakanthan Pakkiyarajah, and Sohrab Hura, who is included in the 2026 Venice Biennale. Address : 2/1, Hindustan Road, Dover Terrace, Ballygunge, Kolkata, West Bengal 700019, India

Jhaveri Contemporary, Mumbai Image Credit: Mohammed Chiba/Courtesy Jhaveri Contemporary Amrita Jhaveri helped set up Christie’s office in India in the mid-1990s and led it for a few years before moving to London, where she worked as an adviser managing private and corporate art collections. In 2010, she cofounded Jhaveri Contemporary with her sister Priya in Mumbai. The gallery moving to its current space, facing the Gateway of India in 2018. Its roster includes a mix of well-known contemporary artists from the South Asian diaspora, including Rana Begum, Lubna Chowdhary, Permindar Kaur, Shezad Dawood, and Mathew Krishanu, as well as the estates of post-modern artists like Mrinalini Mukherjee, Raghubir Singh, Balraj Khanna, Anwar Jalal Shemza, and Zahoor Ul Akhlaq. Address: 3rd Floor, Devidas Mansion, 4 B K Boman Behram Marg, Apollo Bandar, Colaba, Mumbai 400001, India

Nature Morte, New Delhi and Mumbai Image Credit: Akik Rahaman/Courtesy the artists and Nature Morte Nature Morte has umbilical ties to New York. Cofounded by American artist and curator Peter Nagy in East Village in the early 80s, it was reincarnated in 1997 in New Delhi after Nagy had moved there. In 2013, entrepreneur Aparajita Jain became a partner and director in the gallery, helping Nagy, who died in October 2026, take Nature Morte to new heights. In 2021, it moved to two new spaces in Delhi and then in 2024 it expanded to Mumbai. Its roster includes internationally recognised artists like Bharti Kher, Subodh Gupta, Imran Qureshi, Sagarika Sundaram, and Asim Waqif, who represented India at the 2026 Venice Biennale. Address: A-9, Block A, Gulmohar Park, New Delhi, 110049, India

Project 88, Mumbai Image Credit: Anil Rane/Courtesy the artist and Project 88 Artists on gallerist Sree Banerjee Goswami’s roster have routinely found critical recognition in recent years. Rohini Devasher became the first Indian artist to be named Artist of the Year by Deutsche Bank in 2024, the same year Ohida Khandakar won the V&A’s Jameel Prize. Neha Choksi, who like Devasher has been with Project 88 since its inception in 2006, saw the entirety of her last solo at gallery acquired by the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art (KNMA). And Goswami began representing Amol Patil, just before he showed at Documenta 15 in 2022. Other key artists include Delhi-based RAQS Media Collective who also curated the 2016 Shanghai Biennale, and Baroda-based painter Mahesh Baliga. Address: Ground Floor, BMP Building, N.A. Sawant Marg (Narayan A Sawant Road), Colaba, Mumbai – 400 005, Maharashtra, India

Talwar Gallery, New York and New Delhi Image Credit: ©Ranjani Shettar/Courtesy Talwar Gallery, New York and New Delhi/The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York Founded by Deepak Talwar in New York in 2001 and with a second location in New Delhi since 2007, Talwar Gallery has championed art from the Indian subcontinent with several milestones to its credit, from staging Nasreen Mohamedi’s first solo in the US in 2003 to debuting, in 2017, Arpita Singh’s early turn to abstraction in 2017. What sets the gallery apart is tighter artist roster of 13 and a focus on doing fewer shows with longer runs, typically six months, allowing them to focus on cultivating relationships with institutions and collectors as opposed to participating in numerous art fairs each year. One such example is artist Ranjani Shettar whom Talwar started representing two decades ago when she was in her 20s and whose works he has placed in the collections of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Museum of Modern Art, and the San Francisco Museum of Art. Address: C-84 Neeti Bagh, New Delhi – 110049 India

TARQ, Mumbai Image Credit: Courtesy TARQ In 2014 when she was only 25, Hena Kapadia founded TARQ in the Dhanraj Mahal, a heritage building that is home to the Mumbai outposts of Christie’s and Nature Morte. To match the gallery’s growth, she moved to a larger 3000–square-foot space in the city’s Fort neighborhood in 2022. The gallery’s participation in Art Basel Hong Kong since 2018 has led to increased exposure of its artists in East Asia, with M+ acquiring works by Sameer Kulavoor and Parag Tandel. Its roster also includes photographers Ronny Sen and Phillipe Calia, textile artists Boshudhara Mukherjee and Areez Katki, printmaker Soghra Khorasani, painter Rithika Merchant, and draughtsman Vishwa Shroff. Address: Ground Floor, KK (Navsari) Chambers, 39/39B AK Nayak Marg, Fort, Mumbai, Maharashtra 400001, India

Vadehra Art Gallery, New Delhi Image Credit: Courtesy Vadehra Art Gallery Founded in 1987, Vadehra Art Galleryestablished itself by championing modern masters, like M.F. Husain, S.H Raza, Tyeb Mehta, and Ram Kumar. Today, its roster also includes younger South Asian artists like Biraaj Dodiya, Zaam Arif and Ashfika Rehman. In 2011, it added a second space in New Delhi’s Defence Colony neighborhood. The gallery has regularly participated in Art Basel, Art Basel Hong Kong, and Frieze London, where it often stages pop-up shows at Frieze’s 9 Cork Street in Mayfair. Gallery artists like Gauri Gill and Sunil Gupta have had their work acquired by institutions like Tate and the Met, respectively. Address: D-40, Block D, Defence Colony, New Delhi, Delhi 110024, India
excerpt_original: A look at the country’s leading galleries with influential and cutting-edge programs.

article_text:
ポンペイ「青の間」顔料代は、ローマ兵年収の最大9割!? 最新調査結果が発表｜2024年にポンペイで発見された「青の間」の最新調査により、壁を覆う顔料の使用量と価値が明らかになった。その費用はローマ兵の年収の最大約9割に相当するとされ、当時の富裕層による豪奢な装飾の実態が浮かび上がった。【続きを読む】 Photo: Facebook/Archaeological Park of Pompeii

ポンペイ考古学公園で2024年に発見された「青の間」。Photo: Facebook/Archaeological Park of Pompeii

ポンペイの家族を襲った悲劇が明らかに。ドアをベッドで封鎖し最期まで抵抗を試みる｜考古学者たちがポンペイ遺跡にある「ヘレとフリクソスの家」を調査したところ、子ども1人を含む4人の遺骨が見つかった。調査を進めたところ、突然の災害から最期の瞬間まで生き延びようとした家族の物語が明らかになった。【続きを読む】Photo: Courtesy Pompeii Archaeological Park

「ヘレとフリクソスの家」の食堂。Photo: Facebook/Pompeii Archaeological Park

「ヘレとフリクソスの家」の食堂。Photo: Facebook/Pompeii Archaeological Park

「ヘレとフリクソスの家」の室内。Photo: Facebook/Pompeii Archaeological Park

「ヘレとフリクソスの家」の寝室で見つかった木製ベッドの石膏型。Photo: Facebook/Pompeii Archaeological Park

CTスキャンでポンペイ「逃亡者の庭」の犠牲者の職業が判明──携えていたのは「医療箱」｜西暦79年のヴェスヴィオ火山噴火の惨状を今に伝えるポンペイの遺跡「逃亡者の庭」。そこに残された14人の犠牲者のうち、うずくまった男性の職業が最新研究によって明らかになった。【続きを読む】Photo: Ivan Romano/Getty Images

ポンペイ近郊「ポッパエアの別荘」で鮮やかなフレスコ画を発見。孔雀や仮面の精細な描写が姿を現す｜ポンペイに近いトッレ・アヌンツィアータで発掘が進む遺跡で、ポッパエア・サビナの別荘からポンペイ第2様式のフレスコ画が新たに見つかった。ポッパエアは、古代ローマ帝国第5代皇帝・ネロの2番目の妻。【続きを読む】 ポッパエアの別荘で発見された孔雀のフレスコ画（部分）。Courtesy of the Archaeological Park of Pompeii

古代都市ポンペイはどのように消え、いつ発見されたのか。「時が止まった」遺跡の謎を解く｜ヴェスヴィオ火山の火砕流に飲み込まれ、一瞬にして灰の中に消えたポンペイ。古代の時間が閉じ込められたこの遺跡は、今も人々の好奇心を刺激してやまない。近年も次々と新事実が明らかになるポンペイの基礎知識をまとめた。【続きを読む】Photo: LightRocket via Getty Image

ポンペイ遺跡の一区画「貞淑な恋人たちの島」に現存するフレスコ画が、新たな発見と発掘作業を経て一般に初公開された。LightRocket via Getty Images

ポンペイ遺跡にある古代ローマの円形劇場。KONTROLAB/LightRocket via Getty

ポンペイの犠牲者は、なぜ真夏に毛織物を着ていたのか──「死の文化」研究チームの最新調査が示す謎｜西暦79年8月25日に起きたとされるヴェスヴィオ山の噴火。スペインの研究チームによる最新調査で、ポンペイの犠牲者たちは、真夏には不釣り合いとも思える毛織物を身にまとっていた事実が浮かび上がった。【続きを読む】 Photo: University of Valencia

スペイン・バレンシア大学の研究チームによるポンペイ犠牲者の調査風景。Photo: University of Valencia

ポンペイに12メートルの塔があった!? 最新デジタル調査で「失われた街」の真実の姿が明らかに｜ポンペイ考古学公園は、新たなデジタル研究によって、有名な邸宅「Casa del Tiaso（ティアソスの家）」が12メートルにおよぶ塔を備えた多層建築物であった可能性が高いことが分かったと発表した。【続きを読む】 ティアソスの家の3Dデジタルモデル。Photo: Courtesy Pompeii Reset

ポンペイの食堂跡からエジプト由来の陶器を発見。古代の文化交流を明かす重要な手がかりに｜ポンペイの食堂跡から、約2000年前に作られた陶器が発見された。エジプト・アレクサンドリアで作られたとされるこの器が庶民が利用する食堂で見つかったことで、当時の文化交流の実態が浮かび上がる。【続きを読む】 Photo: Courtesy Archeological Park of Pompeii

ポンペイで1世紀ぶりに「デュオニソスの秘儀」の絵を発見｜古代ローマの都市ポンペイの遺跡で、宴会場として使用されていた部屋の3つの壁面にまたがる巨大なフレスコ画が発見された。「デュオニソスの秘儀」を描いたと考えられ、西暦79年に発生したヴェスヴィオ火山噴火の100年以上前のものと推測されている。【続きを読む】Photo: Courtesy of the Pompeii Archaeological Park

古代ローマ以前の巨大な墓地を北イタリアで発見｜イタリアの山岳地帯にあるトレントのサンタ・クローチェで、200基の墓がある大規模な埋葬地が発掘された。発見された副葬品から、埋葬地を造った人々が当時のイタリア半島における他の集団から文化的な影響を受けていたか、交流があったとをみられる。【続きを読む】Photo: Courtesy of the Press Office of the Provincial Council of Trento

炭化した巻物に「愚か」や「生命」などの文字が。AIによる古代文書の開封に進展｜X線画像とAI技術を用い、炭化した古代ローマ文書を解読する試みが新たな進展を見せた。ヘルクラネウムの巻物と呼ばれる文書の「バーチャル開封」と判読に取り組んでいるのは、ヴェスヴィオ・チャレンジの参加者だ。【続きを読む】Photo: Courtesy the Vesuvius Challenge

イタリアのナポリ国立図書館が所蔵するヘルクラネウム・パピルス（2019年撮影）。Photo: Antonio Masiello/Getty Images

火山噴火の悲惨さを物語る足跡をポンペイ近くの工事現場で発見｜イタリア・カンパニア州でメタンガス用パイプラインの改修工事を行っていた際に、ヴェスヴィオ火山噴火の悲惨さが伺える人の足跡や、古代末期に作られたとされる墓跡が発見された。これらの遺跡は、青銅器時代から古代末期までさかのぼるという。【続きを読む】Photo: Soprintendenza Archeologia Belle Arti e Paesaggio di Salerno e Avellino

editorial_excerpt_zh: 为纪念与首尔合作机构交流20周年，东京艺术与空间（TOKAS）将举办由5位日韩艺术家带来的“TOKAS Project Vol. 9‘在场之再演’”。展览从“再演”的视角切入历史、生命、身体与社会等对象，重新审视当下的生存状态。 The post TOKAS Project Vol. 9“在场之再演” @ 东京艺术与空间本乡 first appeared on ART iT（アートイット） .

Project”的第9期展览——“在场之再演”。自2006年起，TOKAS便与首尔的4家合作机构携手，持续开展艺术家的互派工作。为纪念这段交流20周年，本展将以曾参与驻留项目的日韩艺术家为核心，介绍5位以自身身体经验为轴心来重新编织现实的艺术家。在艺术史上，人类一直试图将眼前世界与生命的存续从时间长河中剥离，通过绘画、雕塑、摄影以及电影／影像将其固定，作为永恒的生命延续下来。此外，戏剧、舞蹈和行为艺术等现场艺术，也一直在通过表演者的身体表演，探索在现实世界中让生命当场现前的可能。本展从“再演”的视角捕捉历史、生命、人类、身体和社会等多元对象，通过虚构、雕塑、数字媒体以及身体表现等实践，将艺术家们各自从不同视角观察到的生命形态再次树立在展陈空间中。这并非单纯地临摹现实、再現过去，而是包含当时记忆与情感等固有身体经验的现实加以肉体化，并将其作为进行时态来把握，从而重新思考当下的生存状态。展览围绕不同艺术家的创作，由以下主题构成：“历史的再演”、“生命联结的再演”、“技术对人类的再演”、“旦角身体性的再演”以及“当代社会中的身体感知的再演”。", theater）的形式作为装置进行“上演”，促使人们将围绕日韩关系的这段历史不再视为客观事实，而是作为自己当前的现实来重新审视。 金度希（1979年生于韩国釜山）关注“作为物质的身体”所产生的摩擦和热量等动态能量，探索这些能量的传导路径，并通过让自己的身体介入其中，试图捕捉自我与他者、人工与自然、生与死之间界限变得模糊的转瞬即逝的时刻。比起引发即时反应，她更侧重于揭示随时间推移而堆积的能量所形成的感知层。现居首尔。2006年毕业于弘益大学（美术学）。主要展览包括“Boundaries Resonate, Life Overflows”（金海市立美术馆，金海，韩国，2026）、“Chanting the Hen’s Dream: Phantom Sensation”（杨州艺术工作室777驻地，杨州，韩国，2025）、“The Sound of Light Surface”（城北青年艺术空间，首尔，2024）等。2018年度双边交流项目期间曾入驻TOKAS驻地。自2018年起，她将目光投向象征人类生命之源的“肚脐”，持续开展为人们的肚脐制作模具的项目“Navel Mountain”，并通过此过程中产生的交流，创造出一个体认到由无数人际关系构成的生命联结的场域。在本展中，她将发表扩展了肚脐母题的钟雕塑作品《Navel "朴玟河（1985年生于韩国首尔）以基于实际事件与资料的严密调研为基础，将科幻与纪录片相融合，通过电影、影像装置、出版物、声音作品等多元实践，探索解码塑造人们感知世界的框架并揭示隐藏的故事。她尤其对衍生自科学、历史和媒体技术的视听副产物——光学谱系产生兴趣，通过追溯出现在物件、场所或在线档案中的副产物，试图发现其中寄宿的如同幽灵般不可见者的声音，并通过故事将其可视化。现居首尔。2013年毕业于加州艺术学院（美术）。主要活动包括“CPH:DOX 2025 NEW VISION AWARD”（夏洛滕堡美术馆，哥本哈根，2025）、“The Second Life”（爱马仕工作室，首尔，2025）、“Foreverism: Endless Horizons”（一民美术馆，首尔，2024）等。2025年度双城交流项目期间曾入驻TOKAS驻地。在本展中，面对科技企业对效率与精度的追求等资本主义欲望导致人类劳动被机器人或AI替代、人类受制于技术超生产力的现实，她通过影像作品发问：什么是无法还原为数字的人性？什么是生命？ 殷在弼（1991年生于韩国原州）通过移住记忆的视角探索“归属”与“故乡”的含义，聚焦于难以轻易翻译的个人情感与边缘历史。通过解构传统、现代性以及常由西方中心主义社会定义的男性化与女性化概念的边界，带来超越语言解释的感官体验。生活和工作于韩国和荷兰。2017年毕业于中央大学（首尔）摄影系，2021年修完桑德伯格研究所艺术与设计专业。主要活动包括行为艺术“Blue Night, Blue Shadows”（西首尔市立美术馆，首尔，2026）、行为艺术／个展“Red Celebration”（Vleeshal当代艺术中心，米德尔堡，荷兰，2025）等。自2020年起，因偶然接触到京剧名旦梅兰芳构思的、记录了12种旦角表演姿势与53个手部动作的记录集，从而开始研究旦角，并在现存极少数京剧旦角师父的指导下打磨表演技艺，通过自己的身体重新演绎梅兰芳的身段，借此探索不受生物学性别束缚的跨性别（cross-gender）身体感知。在本展中，他试图通过体现梅兰芳舞蹈的行为表演以及铜版画作品，让昔日的旦角形象在当代复苏。本展为其首次在日本发表作品。 具东希（1974年生于韩国首尔）以日常生活中的不经意事件、电视、互联网以及都市生活等身边的碎片化元素为素材，在对其进行采样的同时重构作品，并在其中介入荒诞而奇异的现象，从而撼动人们的知觉，浮现出理所当然之中潜藏的违和感。在创作过程中，她刻意设置即兴的突发事件或游戏般的规则来营造紧张感，并招致无法预测的发展。其特点是融合了影像、写真、雕塑等不同媒介的装置，它并不直接暗示特定的政治或社会课题，而是以幽默且具讽刺意味的方式探讨社会系统的局限性。现居首尔。1998年毕业于弘益大学雕刻系，2000年修完耶鲁大学美术学院研究生院（雕刻）。主要展览包括“Dear Alexa”（首尔市立美术馆南首尔分馆，首尔，2026）、“Tabula Rasa”（Audio Visual Pavilion Lab，首尔，2023）、“Delivery”（阿尔松尼美术馆，首尔，2019）等。2007年度双边交流项目期间曾入驻东京奇观场地青山。在本展中，她通过探讨顺从于超信息化社会的现代人意识与感知的影像作品，扰动在社会日常生活之中形成的身体习性与固化规范。 Project」の9回目となる「在ることの再演」を開催する。TOKASは2006年よりソウルの4つの提携機関と協働し、相互にアーティストの派遣を行なってきた。その交流20周年を記念する本展では、過去にレジデンス・プログラムに参加した日韓のアーティストを中心に、自身の身体経験を軸に現実を紡ぎ直す5名を紹介する。 芸術の歴史において、人間は目の前に在る世界や生命の存在を時の流れから引き離し、絵画や彫刻、写真や映画／映像によって固定し、永遠の生としてつなぎとめようとしてきた。また演劇や舞踊、パフォーマンスといったライブ・アートは、パフォーマーの身体的な演技を通じて、現実世界における生をその場に現前化することを探求してきた。本展では、歴史、生命、人間、身体、社会といった多様な対象を「再演」の視点から捉え、アーティストたちがそれぞれ異なる視点から観察した生の姿を、フィクション、彫刻、デジタルメディア、身体表現などの実践をとおして展示空間に再び立ち上げる。単に現実を写しとり過去を再現するのではなく、その時の記憶や感情といった固有の身体経験を含めた現実を肉体化し、現在進行形のものとして捉えることで、今日における生の在り様を再考する。展示は、作家ごとに「歴史の再演」「生命のつながりの再演」「テクノロジーによる人間の再演」「女形の身体性の再演」「現代社会における身体感覚の再演」と題したテーマで構成される。"}, かわす・つくる・ともにいる―生きるための回路」（アーツ前橋、群馬、2026）、「山本卓卓＆三野新『ここに立ち、ここに立つ』」（サッポロ・パラレル・ミュージアム、北海道、2024）、「外が静かになるまで」（十和田市現代美術館 space、青森、2023）などがある。2025年度二都市間交流事業プログラムでSeMAナンジ・レジデンシーに滞在した。本展では、韓国の龍山米軍基地や戦後の占領期に関する歴史のリサーチ、戦争が現在の日常生活や身体に及ぼしている影響への考察をもとに書き下ろした戯曲「温室／オンシル」の舞台となる温室を展示空間に立ち上げる。「石」「鉄」「トラック」という三つのモノの会話によって紡がれる物語を、オブジェクト・シアターの手法によってインスタレーションとして「上演」し、日本と韓国の関係をめぐる歴史を、客観的な事実としてではなく、現在の自分自身の現実として捉え直すことを促す。 キム・ドヒ TOKAS Project Vol. 9「在ることの再演」 2026年10月3日（土）–11月8日（日） トーキョーアーツアンドスペース本郷 https://www.tokyoartsandspace.jp/ 開館時間：11:00–19:00（入場は閉館30分前まで） 休館日：月（ただし、10/12は開館）、10/13 展覧会URL： https://www.tokyoartsandspace.jp/archive/exhibition/2026/20261003-7578.html 出品作家：ウン・ジェピル、キム・ドヒ、ク・ドンヒ、パク・ミンハ、三野新

トーキョーアーツアンドスペース（TOKAS）では、国際的な交流を促進し、多文化的な視点で多様なテーマについて思考する展覧会プログラム「TOKAS Project」の9回目となる「在ることの再演」を開催する。TOKASは2006年よりソウルの4つの提携機関と協働し、相互にアーティストの派遣を行なってきた。その交流20周年を記念する本展では、過去にレジデンス・プログラムに参加した日韓のアーティストを中心に、自身の身体経験を軸に現実を紡ぎ直す5名を紹介する。 芸術の歴史において、人間は目の前に在る世界や生命の存在を時の流れから引き離し、絵画や彫刻、写真や映画／映像によって固定し、永遠の生としてつなぎとめようとしてきた。また演劇や舞踊、パフォーマンスといったライブ・アートは、パフォーマーの身体的な演技を通じて、現実世界における生をその場に現前化することを探求してきた。本展では、歴史、生命、人間、身体、社会といった多様な対象を「再演」の視点から捉え、アーティストたちがそれぞれ異なる視点から観察した生の姿を、フィクション、彫刻、デジタルメディア、身体表現などの実践をとおして展示空間に再び立ち上げる。単に現実を写しとり過去を再現するのではなく、その時の記憶や感情といった固有の身体経験を含めた現実を肉体化し、現在進行形のものとして捉えることで、今日における生の在り様を再考する。展示は、作家ごとに「歴史の再演」「生命のつながりの再演」「テクノロジーによる人間の再演」「女形の身体性の再演」「現代社会における身体感覚の再演」と題したテーマで構成される。

excerpt_original: トーキョーアーツアンドスペース（TOKAS）では、ソウルの提携機関との交流20周年を記念し、日韓5名のアーティストによる「TOKAS Project Vol. 9『在ることの再演』」を開催する。歴史や生命、身体、社会といった対象を「再演」の視点から捉え、今日における生の在り様を再考する。 The post TOKAS Project Vol. 9「在ることの再演」 @ トーキョーアーツアンドスペース本郷 first appeared on ART iT（アートイット） .
